paragraphs.text: About 20% of world electricity production capacity is gas-fired, and over the last two decades gas plants have been widely chosen for new capacity, especially in developed countries, because they combine high efficiency, low installed cost, good reliability and flexibility. Shale gas supply and growing doubts about nuclear power in some countries have recently raised interest further. Moving from coal to gas cuts power-sector emissions considerably but does not remove CO2, so deep long-term cuts will probably require new gas plants to be built and run with CO2 capture and storage (CCS). Because CCS work has focused mostly on coal and little has been published on gas plant performance and cost with CCS, IEAGHG commissioned Parsons Brinckerhoff to carry out this techno-economic study of CO2 capture at natural gas fired power plants.

Six natural gas combined cycle configurations are evaluated for performance and cost: (1) a reference plant with no CO2 capture; (2) post combustion capture by scrubbing with non-proprietary MEA solvent; (3) post combustion scrubbing with an advanced proprietary amine solvent; (4) recycle of cooled flue gas to the gas turbine inlet combined with MEA post combustion scrubbing; (5) an integrated plant with natural gas reforming and pre-combustion scrubbing; and (6) reforming with pre-combustion scrubbing, underground buffer storage of hydrogen-rich gas and a separate combined cycle plant. The proprietary solvent case stands for the type of solvent several suppliers are developing; MHI and Siemens supplied information, but the case is not a model of any one vendor's technology.

In the pre-combustion cases natural gas undergoes air blown partial oxidation followed by shift conversion, and CO2 is removed with Selexol solvent. One variant places the reformer and combined cycle on the same site. In the other, the reformer/CO2 capture plant and the power plant sit on separate sites, with an underground salt cavern holding 6 weeks of buffer storage of the hydrogen/nitrogen fuel gas; the study contractor supplied the underground hydrogen storage cost data from its experience building such facilities in the USA. Performance was assessed with process and thermal plant simulation tools (AspenPlus®, GTPRO®, GTMASTER® and Thermoflex®). Equipment lists and plant layout drawings, together with in-house cost data and vendor information, gave high-level capital and operating cost estimates, which then fed an economic model used to compare the plants and test sensitivity to key economic parameters. The report covers plant design, power output, efficiency, greenhouse gas intensity, capital and O&M costs, levelised cost of electricity and CO2 avoidance cost, and includes process flow diagrams, stream data, equipment lists and layout diagrams.

The main base case assumptions (detailed in the main report) are: a greenfield site at a coastal location in the Netherlands; 2 GE9FB gas turbines plus 1 steam turbine; 9°C ambient temperature; mechanical draught cooling towers; base load operation; natural gas at €6/GJ on an LHV basis (€5.42/GJ HHV basis); 2011 costs; an 8% discount rate in constant money; a 25 year operating life; 4 years of construction; CO2 storage cost of €5/t; and a CO2 emission cost of €10/t. Sensitivities to several economic parameters were also run. Net outputs are roughly 800MW but differ between cases, since gas turbines come only in fixed sizes and ancillary steam and power demands vary, being much higher where CO2 is captured.

Levelised electricity costs assume fuel and other prices stay constant in real terms and that capacity factor is constant over the plant life, except for a reduced capacity factor in year one. The cost of CO2 avoidance compares CO2 emitted per kWh and electricity cost (with CO2 emission charges excluded) between gas fired plants with and without capture; choosing a different reference plant, such as an unabated coal fired plant, would change this figure.

paragraphs.section: Overview: Results and Discussion - Plant performance
paragraphs.text: For conventional MEA post combustion capture the efficiency penalty splits into 4.8 percentage points from steam extracted for solvent regeneration, 1.3 percentage points from capture plant auxiliary power (chiefly the flue gas booster fan) and 1.7 percentage points from CO2 compression. The proprietary solvent loses less efficiency mostly because it needs 19% less regeneration steam; its regeneration heat demand is 2700kJ/kg CO2 captured. With flue gas recycle the penalty is also smaller than the MEA base case, because capture plant ancillary power drops by 21% (mostly lower flue gas fan power) and steam use by 6%; part of this gain is lost because warmer recycled flue gas replacing some intake air raises the gas turbine compressor inlet temperature and lowers combined cycle efficiency. Turbine makers have run successful combustor tests with flue gas recycle and it is under trial in a large commercial gas turbine. The study assumes 50% recycle to show the upper bound of the benefit, though combustor design may limit recycle to lower rates.

paragraphs.section: Overview: Results and Discussion - Plant performance
paragraphs.text: Overall energy use is much higher for pre-combustion capture than for post combustion. Natural gas pre-combustion plants offer many design choices: air or purified oxygen as oxidant, chemical or physical CO2 solvent, oxidant taken from the gas turbine compressor or from a dedicated compressor, and numerous heat integration schemes. The contractor selected options by weighing efficiency, capital cost, capture percentage, risk and operability, and on that basis accepted roughly 81.5% capture for the pre-combustion cases versus 90% for post combustion, while noting a higher capture rate could be designed for if required.

paragraphs.section: Overview: Results and Discussion - Plant performance
paragraphs.text: In future grids containing much other low-CO2 generation (coal with CCS, wind, solar, nuclear and so on), gas plants with CCS will usually have higher marginal running costs because of fuel cost, so they are expected to run below base load and must operate flexibly at lower annual capacity factors. Because IEAGHG has recently reported on operating flexibility of capture plants (IEAGHG report 2012/6, June 2012), a separate detailed flexibility assessment was not repeated, but part load was examined at 40% gas turbine load, which gives about 50% of total net output. There, plants with and without post combustion capture were estimated to have thermal efficiencies 6-7 percentage points below their 100% load values; a footnote warns that the part load penalty may differ for other manufacturers' gas turbines. A gas plant with a low average capacity factor need not spend much time at low load: it may mostly run near full load or stay shut down to avoid the part load efficiency loss.

paragraphs.section: Overview: Results and Discussion - Base case costs
paragraphs.text: Capital costs are given as EPC (Engineering, Procurement and Construction) costs, which leave out owner's costs and interest during construction; those items are nonetheless included when the levelised cost of electricity (LCOE) is calculated. The base load LCOEs include CO2 transport and storage and CO2 emission charges. Assumed annual capacity factors reflect expected availability: 93% without capture, 90% with post combustion capture and 85% with pre-combustion capture. The cost of CO2 emission avoidance is defined as the carbon price at which plants with and without CCS would produce electricity at equal cost.

paragraphs.section: Overview: Results and Discussion - Base case costs
paragraphs.text: Costs for both the proprietary solvent and flue gas recycle cases are well below the conventional MEA case, chiefly owing to better thermal efficiency and smaller equipment, plus cheaper solvent in the proprietary case. Combining flue gas recycle with a proprietary solvent should raise efficiency further and lower cost, but this was outside the scope and is suggested for a later study. Pre-combustion capture is clearly more expensive than post combustion. The hydrogen/nitrogen storage case is reported at base load only for comparability, although its real benefit would appear at lower capacity factors (covered under sensitivities). Its capital cost exceeds the pre-combustion case without storage because of the storage facilities, equivalent to €218/kW, and the extra cost of having separate reforming/capture and power plants.

paragraphs.section: Overview: Results and Discussion - Base case costs
paragraphs.text: Figure 1 breaks down the levelised cost of electricity for each case; fuel is the largest component everywhere. Capture plants have higher fuel costs because their efficiency is lower, but the main driver of their higher total cost is larger capital charges. Figure 1 caption: Levelised costs of electricity, base load operation (components shown: fuel, capital charges, O+M, overheads, CO2 emission cost, CO2 transport and storage).

paragraphs.section: Overview: Results and Discussion - Cost sensitivities
paragraphs.text: Sensitivities were run for every plant; the post combustion proprietary solvent case is used as the example in Figures 2 and 3, which show electricity and CO2 abatement costs at high, medium and low values of each parameter, with other plants covered in the main report. Figure 2 caption: Electricity cost sensitivities (post combustion capture, proprietary solvent), with parameter values CO2 emission cost (0, 10, 100 €/t), CO2 transport and storage (0, 5, 20 €/t), discount rate (5, 8, 10%), fuel price (3, 6, 12 €/GJ) and capacity factor (90, 50, 25%).

paragraphs.section: Overview: Results and Discussion - Cost sensitivities
paragraphs.text: Electricity cost reacts most strongly to fuel price and annual capacity factor; the broad 3-12 €/GJ fuel price range reflects large uncertainty in future gas prices and regional differences. The base €5/t CO2 transport and storage cost may correspond to onshore storage near the plant; with enhanced oil recovery (EOR) the net cost could be zero or negative, while raising it to €20/t for distant offshore storage affects electricity cost only modestly. Gas plants benefit relative to coal here since they store roughly half as much CO2 per MWh.

paragraphs.section: Overview: Results and Discussion - Cost sensitivities
paragraphs.text: Lowering capacity factor from 90% to 50% raises costs moderately, but going further to 25% has a much larger effect. Most other low-CO2 options (renewables, nuclear, etc.) carry high fixed costs, so their electricity cost climbs faster as capacity factor falls, which should give gas plants with CCS an edge in intermediate load generation, a sizeable share of total electricity. In the capacity factor sensitivity the plant is assumed to run at full load part of the time and be shut down otherwise, though real plants may sometimes run at part load; start-up, shutdown and part-load cost penalties were not included as they were out of scope and depend on the operating schedule.

paragraphs.section: Overview: Results and Discussion - Cost sensitivities
paragraphs.text: The base CO2 emission cost of €10/t roughly matches current typical EU levels but is below what would make CCS economically attractive. Even €100/t would change the cost of electricity with CCS only slightly, as it applies only to the 10% of CO2 left uncaptured.

paragraphs.section: Overview: Results and Discussion - Cost sensitivities
paragraphs.text: Figure 3 caption: CO2 abatement cost sensitivities (post combustion capture, proprietary solvent), for CO2 transport and storage (0, 5, 20 €/t), discount rate (5, 8, 10%), fuel price (3, 6, 12 €/GJ) and capacity factor (90, 50, 25%). Across this wide range the abatement cost mostly stays between about 55 and 85 €/t CO2, because apart from transport and storage cost the parameters affect the no-capture reference plant as well as the capture plant; combined parameter changes could fall outside this band. The 25% capacity factor case is the one exception, with markedly higher cost.

paragraphs.section: Overview: Results and Discussion - Cost sensitivities
paragraphs.text: Since gas plants are generally expected to run below base load, capacity factor sensitivity matters most, so Figure 4 (Sensitivity to annual capacity factor) gives electricity costs for every case at base load, 50% and 25% capacity factor. At 25% the costs of post combustion capture and pre-combustion capture with hydrogen storage are roughly equal. A footnote explains that the overview assumes the storage case has one continuously running reforming and capture plant supplying several combined cycle plants at lower capacity factors, whereas the main report assumes the reformer feeds a single combined cycle plant and also runs at 25% capacity factor. Earlier IEAGHG work (Davison, Energy Procedia 4 (2011) 2548-2555) suggests hydrogen storage pre-combustion capture suits coal better, with breakeven against post combustion reached at a much higher capacity factor, so further hydrogen storage work is recommended for coal or biomass plants.

Reviewers from the power industry and research bodies with post and pre combustion capture experience at gas plants, along with some post combustion technology vendors, commented on the draft, and the report was revised accordingly. Overall they judged it of high quality and broadly in line with other recent gas plant capture studies. Several stressed the importance of NGCC operating flexibility and wanted more on it; this is partly addressed by a separate IEAGHG flexibility report and could be studied further, and the overview gives more weight to low capacity factor operation in response.

Post combustion capture lowers NGCC thermal efficiency by about 7-8 percentage points, raises capital cost per kW by about 80-120% and raises base load electricity cost by about 30-40%. In the cheapest case studied (post combustion with a proprietary solvent) the CO2 emission avoidance cost, i.e. the carbon price giving equal base load electricity cost with and without CCS, is about €65/tonne; it may be lower against an alternative baseline such as a coal plant. Recycling part of the cooled flue gas to the compressor inlet increases CO2 concentration at the capture unit and could improve efficiency by up to 0.3 percentage points and cut electricity cost by up to 8 percent. NGCC with CCS may run below base load, especially alongside much other low-CO2 generation; in the cheapest case a 50% capacity factor lifts avoidance cost to €87/tonne. With current technology, pre-combustion capture for NGCC is not economically competitive with post combustion capture.

Recommended follow-up work: extend the study to combine a high efficiency proprietary post combustion solvent with gas turbine flue gas recycle; evaluate gas plants with other capture technologies (other liquid solvents, solid sorbents, membranes) once enough input data exist; study how gas plants with CCS would operate in future systems with large amounts of other low-CO2 generation; and have IEAGHG carry out a new study of baseline coal fired plants with CO2 capture.

Gas-fired generation makes up roughly 20% of world electricity production capacity and over the past twenty years has been the preferred technology for new capacity, especially in developed countries. Modern combined cycle gas turbine (CCGT) plants reach fuel efficiencies of 50 to 60%, installed capital cost is relatively low at around EUR450/kW to EUR700/kW, and the plants are reliable and flexible, able to follow demand swings or fuel price changes quickly so operators can maximise revenue from electricity market price opportunities.

Gas generation also matters for climate policy. Energy accounts for 60% of all greenhouse gas emissions, and without major policy change energy-related emissions are expected to grow 57% by 2030. Gas has a far lower Greenhouse Intensity than coal: a typical CCGT emits about 370kgCO2/MWh versus roughly 750 to 900kgCO2/MWh for a black coal station. The UK Government's Electricity Market Reform White Paper stresses new gas plant in the near term and, via a carbon price floor and an emissions performance standard, aims to cut UK generation CO2 substantially as old coal plant closes; much of the replacement is expected to be new-build gas plant over the next 8 to 10 years.

Switching to gas lowers power sector emissions considerably but is not CO2-free, so in the longer term new gas plant will need to be built and run with carbon capture and storage (CCS). The IEA Energy Technology Perspectives BLUE Map target of 14Gt CO2 emissions by 2050, a 50% cut from 2005 levels, is achievable only with broad deployment of Gas + CCS alongside renewables, new nuclear, Coal + CCS and various energy efficiency and demand side measures.

Figure 1 caption: BLUE map emissions reduction plan (generation by source in PWh for 2007, Baseline 2050 and BLUE Map 2050). Since that plan was drawn up in 2008, estimates of world gas reserves have been revised sharply upward thanks to technology for extracting gas from shale rock. US reserves are now estimated at about 100 rather than 30 years of current consumption, and analysts consider the US market oversupplied. The US DOE Energy Information Administration's March 2011 long term forecast put gas at around USD4.5/GJ, against USD12/GJ forecast in 2007 for 2011. After the Fukushima accident in Japan and decisions by several governments not to replace ageing nuclear plants, gas is strongly expected to take a larger share of the future energy mix.

CCS work in power generation has so far targeted coal plant emissions, where impact is greatest: of 77 large-scale integrated CCS projects (LSIP) in development, more than 53% involve coal-fired generation, the biggest share of any sector. Because gas generation will be so important in the future mix, capture must also be demonstrated on gas plants to learn its effects on technical and commercial performance, operating flexibility and running costs. This study examines the technical and economic performance of CO2 capture and compression at new-build gas plants, extending IEA GHG's 2005 work on retrofitting capture to existing gas plants. It aims to give a current, independent benchmark for capture technologies designed for new gas plants and to compare pre- and post-combustion routes, using process and thermal performance simulation, concept design and sizing, cost estimation and economic modelling to evaluate net output (MW e), efficiency (%), Greenhouse Intensity (gCO2/kWh), lifetime cost of electricity (EUR/kWh) and cost of CO2 abatement (EUR/tCO2).

Five scenarios are examined to show how capture technology type, configuration and operation affect these metrics (numbering keeps gaps for unused scenarios 2 and 7): Scenario 1, a CCGT Reference Plant; Scenario 3, CCGT with post-combustion capture; Scenario 4, CCGT with post-combustion capture plus flue-gas recirculation; Scenario 5, a combined cycle plant with natural gas reforming and pre-combustion capture; Scenario 6, a natural gas reforming plant with pre-combustion capture that supplies hydrogen to a remote combined cycle plant or to intermediate storage. For each scenario process and thermal simulation software provide performance and also Heat and Mass balances (HMB), Process Flow Diagrams (PFD), equipment lists, layout drawings and utility consumption lists, which underpin high-level capital and operating cost estimates that are fed into an economic model for comparing scenarios. The report gathers the study conclusions and presents technical and economic results with discussion, key findings and recommendations.

The report runs from introduction and background, through reference plant and capture technology selection, to overviews of Scenarios 3, 4, 5 and 6, then capital cost estimation and economic evaluation, and finally results, discussion, conclusions and recommendations. Figure 2 caption: Report Structure.

Several software platforms were combined: GE Gate-cycle© and Thermoflow GT Pro© for gas and steam turbine performance, and AspenTech© tools for natural gas reforming and for pre and post combustion capture. 1.6.1 Process Plant Performance Modelling: CO2 capture and compression processes were modelled in AspenPlus® (v7.2), a widely used process tool for conceptual design, optimisation and performance monitoring across chemical, oil and gas, metals and minerals, coal and power industries; its large database of pure component and phase equilibrium data for conventional chemicals, electrolytes, solids and polymers makes it suitable for modelling different CO2 separation technologies.

Thermal plant modelling used the Thermoflow Inc. programs GT PRO, GT MASTER and Thermoflex (Version 21). GT PRO holds a database of gas turbines with mapped performance curves and lets an experienced user simulate overall gas turbine and combined cycle performance at design conditions. GT MASTER takes a GT PRO design and evaluates off-design cases such as part-load and different ambient conditions. Thermoflex builds a plant model from individual components, giving much more freedom to evaluate bespoke concepts; a GT PRO model can be imported and broken into components, then modified by adding, removing and linking components, and Thermoflex also has an off-design mode.

For the reference and reforming scenarios, GT PRO handled the design case and GT MASTER the part-load case. The post-combustion capture scenarios needed strong two-way coupling between the thermal plant model and the capture plant process model, mainly the exchange of steam and condensate and the flue gas interfaces. To support iteration and obtain an accurate overall plant model, the whole process was represented in Thermoflex using bespoke design concepts, and this supplied the starting interface parameters for the capture plant process model.

The economic model derives from Parsons Brinckerhoff's Powering the Nation model, built for its Powering the Nation Report (available at http://www.pbworld.com/regional/uk_europe_specialty/). For each generation type it accounts for forecast fuel, carbon and O&M costs, together with optimum economic plant life, operating regime and construction schedule. Performance modelling outputs are fed in to compare the options' economics, and the model yields lifetime cost of electricity, CO2 avoidance cost, operation and maintenance costs and other key parameters.

The design basis follows IEA GHG's standard assessment criteria ('Criteria for Technical and Economic assessment of plants with low CO2 emissions'). The site is coastal, in the north-east Netherlands. Scenarios are sized for about 800MWe net at site ambient conditions, though actual output differs with the thermal and electrical parasitic load of each capture and compression plant. Every scenario uses a 2 + 1 CCGT arrangement: two gas turbines, each exhausting into its own triple-pressure HRSG, supplying steam to a single steam turbine. Power is generated at 50Hz; gross output is the sum of the outputs at all generator terminals before auxiliary loads are deducted, and efficiency is stated on an LHV basis.

Air and water emission limits for SOx, NOx and particulate matter (PM) are those for new power plants in the Netherlands. Under the EU Industrial Emissions Directive (IED) (Directive 2010/75/EU), CCGT plants face strict NOx standards, and the study adopts the IED limit of 50 mg/Nm^3 NOx. A note states this applies to CCGT operation above 70% load, with values referred to 273.15K, 101.3kPa, dry waste gas and a standard O2 content of 15% for gas turbines and gas engines.

To give every scenario a common basis, one reference plant and one common GT were modelled throughout. The reference is a CCGT with a pair of gas turbine generators (GTG) and heat recovery steam generators (HRSG) plus a single steam turbine generator (STG), i.e. a 2 + 1 configuration. All scenarios use 2 + 1 and aim, as far as possible, at about 800MWe net at site conditions, which calls for heavy-duty F-class gas turbines of nominally 270-330 MW ISO rating; the pre-combustion scenarios additionally need GTs able to burn fuel with high hydrogen (H2) content. These needs drove the choice of reference GT, and the chapter reviews the heavy duty GT market as of mid-2011 to identify qualifying manufacturers and justify the selection.

A multi-shaft arrangement of two GTGs, two HRSGs and one STG is used; the choice hardly affects cost or performance estimates, but multi-shaft plants, with their double-flow low pressure steam turbines, are usually considered better suited to post-combustion capture. As is normal for this class, a three-pressure reheat steam system is adopted, with turbine inlet conditions of 600°C/170bara for High Pressure (HP) steam and 600°C/40bara for Hot Reheat (MP or IP) steam. These conditions exceed today's typical values, but the terms of reference (ToR) require technology commercially available in 2020, when many gas plants (with or without CCS) are expected to replace retiring assets; since most OEMs are already considering or demonstrating similar conditions, they are expected to be proven and typical in CCGTs by 2020.

Large 50 Hz GTs on the world market at the time were: Siemens SGT5-4000F (the near-identical Ansaldo AE94.3A left out for simplicity); Siemens SGT5-8000H; General Electric 9FB (the GE 9FB-05 not yet launched, so excluded); Alstom GT26 (its 2011 upgrade not yet launched, so excluded); and the Mitsubishi Heavy Industries 701F4 and 701G2. This market is, and will probably stay, competitive on performance and price, and all of these machines or their successors could suit various scenarios, but a single GT was chosen to make scenarios comparable. The recent growth in 50Hz GTs above 300 MW suggests such units may be standard for large CCGTs by 2020; however, the study takes a cautious view of how soon high-hydrogen combustion versions of the larger machines, needed for the pre-combustion cases, will appear. Each GT is reviewed against the idea of one machine serving all scenarios of Section 1.3, using Gas Turbine World 2011 performance data.

paragraphs.section: 2.2.1.1 Suitability for high H2 content fuel
paragraphs.text: The SGT5-4000F's 60Hz sibling, the SGT6-5000F, is widely considered for US Integrated Gasification Combined Cycle (IGCC) projects, but the SGT5-4000F has a different combustion system and Siemens said at the study's start that it was not developing it for syngas/H2. Its combustor is a single annular unit with burners placed around the circumference, sold as the hybrid burner ring (HBR) because it can run in premix or diffusion mode depending on load; silo and can combustors are generally seen as better than annular ones for high-hydrogen fuels. The first and so far only SGT5-8000H entered commercial CCGT service in mid-2011; it may be common by 2020, but a proven syngas/H2 version by then is uncertain. Siemens says a syngas/hydrogen-capable SGT5-8000H is aimed at future IGCC projects under discussion and could use the same can-type combustors as the 60 Hz SGT6-5000F. Even so, being the newest machine considered, it was judged too early to base a step change such as syngas/H2 combustion on it.

ISO performance of the GE-9FB: Power Output=284MW; Simple Cycle Efficiency=37.9%; Heat Rate=9512 kJ/kWh. 2.2.2.1 Suitability for high H2 content fuel: within a US Department of Energy funded programme GE is developing "FB" syngas combustion systems, whose "FA" syngas predecessors have run for over 15 years on 60Hz GE 7FA gas turbines.

ISO performance of the GT26 (with air quench cooler): Power Output=296.4MW; Simple Cycle Efficiency=39.6%; Heat Rate=9091 kJ/kWh. 2.2.3.1 Suitability for high H2 content fuel: the GT26 has two annular combustors in sequence, each with twenty-four burners, separated by the HP Turbine; EV (EnVironmental) burners are followed by SEV (Sequential EnVironmental) burners. This SEV reheat mode is found only on the GT24 and GT26 and gives a theoretical thermodynamic benefit, achieving high output and efficiency without relying as much on a higher firing temperature. To the authors' knowledge Alstom is not pursuing syngas firing for the GT26, and because of the sequential combustion, commercial GT modelling packages can only model it on pure methane.

ISO performance of the 701F4: Power Output=312.1MW; Simple Cycle Efficiency=39.3%; Heat Rate=9161 kJ/kWh. It first entered commercial service only in 2010, and MHI's active syngas combustion work is all on its G-class GTs. 2.2.5 MHI701G2: ISO Power Output=334.0MW; Simple Cycle Efficiency=39.5%; Heat Rate=9105 kJ/kWh. Its combustors and transition pieces are steam cooled, which makes it inherently less operationally flexible (e.g. slower start-up); with output only a little above the 701F4, it is not marketed in Europe and was dropped from further consideration.
The GE 9FB was chosen as the study's reference GT, being the only listed machine that is both sold in Europe and actively pursued as the basis for a syngas gas turbine.

paragraphs.section: 2.3 Site location and ambient conditions for modelling
paragraphs.text: IEA GHG's standard criteria place the notional site on the coast of the North East Netherlands, and a location near Eemshaven was used for air dispersion modelling. The IEA criteria give 9°C average dry-bulb temperature and 60% relative humidity, but because cooling towers were chosen and coincident humidity strongly affects their sizing, IEA GHG agreed to use a more representative 80% relative humidity. All full and part load simulations used these design average conditions.

Although the site is coastal, many Dutch near-coast CCGTs, and most CCGTs in Europe and worldwide, do not use once-through seawater cooling, so mechanical draught wet cooling towers were chosen to make results widely applicable. Hybrid towers for plume abatement were not chosen, as the need depends on unknown plume effects on neighbouring facilities. For all scenarios the approach between ambient wet bulb temperature and cooling water supply temperature is 7°C, giving a supply temperature of 14.36°C; the design range (rise from supply to return) is 11°C, giving a return temperature of 25.36°C.

The reference plant cost estimate covers the usual CCGT utilities: cylinder nitrogen for purging; cylinder carbon dioxide for fire suppression; instrument air from package compressors (2 x 100%) of nominal 1 t/h; a service water network of 2 inch nominal bore pipe; a water treatment plant with reverse osmosis and de-ionization making 45 t/h of demineralised water; fire water from the raw water tank with one electric and one diesel firewater pump; a package auxiliary boiler mainly for start up; and a 2.5 MW emergency diesel generator for safe shut down.

The layout of the reference CCGT plant follows on the next page as a drawing titled CCGT Referance Plant (No Carbon Capture), drawing number 64225A-DSC-00010, prepared by Parsons Brinckerhoff for the CO2 Capture at Gas Fired Power Plants Study.

Parsons Brinckerhoff has observed major OEMs lowering guaranteed minimum CCGT load in response to demand for flexible plants, so 40% GT load, slightly under 50% CCGT load for the reference case, was considered a suitable part load case for the notional 2020 plant. paragraphs.section: 3. CO2 Capture Processes Suitable for Gas-Fired Power Plants
paragraphs.text: Capture methods for gas plants are generally grouped as post-combustion, which treats the combustion gases leaving the CCGT before they are released to atmosphere, or pre-combustion, which strips the carbon from the natural gas so that the remaining hydrogen is burned. The chapter reviews current best available pre and post combustion techniques, justifies the capture technologies chosen for detailed study, and outlines available CO2 compression options.

paragraphs.section: 3.1 High Level Post Combustion Technology Options
paragraphs.text: Commercially available post-combustion options, which differ in how they separate CO2 from the flue gas, are chemical absorption, physical absorption, adsorption (Pressure/Temperature Swing), gas membrane separation and cryogenic distillation. 3.1.1 Chemical Absorption: both chemical and physical absorption normally circulate a liquid solvent between an absorption step and a desorption (regeneration) step; in chemical absorption the CO2 reacts with the solvent, which boosts its physical dissolution, making the method suitable where CO2 partial pressure is low.
Here CO2 dissolves in particular physical solvents, driven by CO2 partial pressure; when CO2 is below 15% by volume, the pressurisation needed would usually make the option unattractive.

A solid medium takes up CO2 from the flue gas, with sorption and regeneration usually done by cycling pressure or temperature in one vessel. Many such systems have poor selectivity and give impure CO2, so they are normally paired with further steps such as cryogenic distillation to reach the required purity; commercial adsorption capacity is also rather low, which may rule them out for large plants with dilute flue gas. 3.1.4 Gas Membrane Separation: membranes are engineered materials through which a gas permeates selectively, driven by the pressure difference across them; compressing gas turbine flue gas to the needed pressure would make this uneconomic. 3.1.5 Cryogenic Distillation: the gas mixture is liquefied and separated in a distillation column, and because liquefaction uses much energy it suits only high CO2 concentrations.

With today's technology, chemical absorption is the only listed option that copes with the very low CO2 partial pressure of gas plant flue gas (about 4vol% CO2), and this remains true with flue gas recirculation, which can raise CO2 to 8-9vol%.

Amines are common CO2 absorption solvents. MEA, a primary alkanolamine, has been used for CO2 absorption for decades, though at smaller scale than an 800 MWe plant needs. Tertiary alkanolamines such as methyldiethanolamine (MDEA) hold more CO2 than MEA but absorb it more slowly, and blends (e.g. MEA with MDEA) are being studied to balance capacity and rate. Cyclic amines like piperazine also absorb quickly and are used in special blends. Some proprietary solvents, such as KS-1 from Kansai Electric Power Company (KEPCO) and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI), are hindered amines in which the base amine is chemically modified for better performance. Ammonia (Alstom's Chilled Ammonia Process) and amino-acid salts (Siemens' proprietary process) have also been shown to work for CO2 capture.

Relative to most amines, MEA offers fast absorption, fairly cheap solvent, fairly low molecular weight and acceptable thermal stability, but its regeneration energy demand is especially high and would penalise plant performance. Further drawbacks are fairly high corrosion, particularly at high CO2 loading; significant degradation in the presence of O2, SOx and NOx; and evaporation losses from its relatively high vapour pressure. New solvents target these problems: MHI's KS-1 and Siemens' amino-acid salts both need less regeneration energy, and the amino-acid salt also has almost zero vapour pressure and good resistance to oxygen degradation. For these reasons chemical absorption was judged the best post-combustion capture method for the study.

paragraphs.section: 3.3 High Level Pre Combustion Technology Options
paragraphs.text: In the pre-combustion scenarios, synthesis gas downstream of the shift reactors reaches up to about 16vol% CO2 once condensate is knocked out, which opens up more capture options. 3.3.1 Adsorption (Pressure/Temperature Swing): these work better at high pressure, so they fit pre-combustion better than post-combustion; the nearest commercial analogue is pressure swing adsorption for purifying hydrogen from synthesis gas. Some hydrogen fuel may leave with the CO2, and an added step such as cryogenic distillation could purify the CO2 further, raising operating and capital costs.

The higher pressures of pre-combustion make membranes feasible, and their modular nature means scale-up is not a concern, but they lack the usual economies of scale, which may make them unattractive for large capture duties. There is also normally a compromise between CO2 recovery and purity, partly because separating H2 from CO2 with membranes has proved difficult. 3.3.3 Cryogenic Distillation: the energy needed to chill the synthesis gas rules this out, even with pre-combustion CO2 levels. 3.3.4 Chemical absorption: it can capture CO2 at far lower partial pressure (Section 3.1), but solvent regeneration demands much thermal energy, and the high CO2 partial pressure here may not cut that demand enough.

Physical absorption becomes workable at the higher CO2 concentrations of the pre-combustion scenarios and relies on mature processes. Performance depends on CO2 partial pressure, so higher pressures help, and the solvent can be regenerated by pressure reduction or by heating, giving extra efficiency options. The reformer runs at fairly high pressure so the gas turbine inlet pressure is met without compression, which favours physical absorption. Chemical solvents absorb more at low CO2 partial pressure, while physical solvents win above some threshold; sources quote different thresholds, some as low as 4bara. Figure 5 caption: Comparison between Chemical and Physical Solvents (absorption capacity versus partial pressure).

Chemical and physical absorption are both feasible. CO2 partial pressure in the synthesis gas entering the capture plant was about 6bara, below the roughly 20bara typical of IGCC where physical solvents are standard, yet physical absorption can still greatly reduce regeneration steam compared with chemical absorption, freeing steam for better heat integration and overall efficiency; physical processes usually need more electrical power, however. Among available physical solvents, Selexol offers fairly high CO2 solubility and hence high capacity, very low vapour pressure that limits solvent loss, and is non-toxic, non-corrosive and biodegradable.

Reciprocating compressors have compressed CO2 only at about one tenth of this study's scale, so centrifugal compressors, which are generally more efficient and reliable, are chosen for large CCS duties. They come as single shaft in-line machines or multi-shaft integral-gear machines. In the in-line type all impellers are shrunk onto one shaft and turn at one speed, giving easier maintenance access; Rolls Royce is a leading maker. In the integral gear type a driver turns a single bull gear that drives up to five pinion shafts carrying shrunk-on impellers, each at a speed set by its pinion teeth, so impeller speeds can be optimised; Man Diesel & Turbo is a leading maker. Standard multi-shaft integral gear sizes matched the CO2 compression capacities required, so this type was selected.

paragraphs.section: 4. Overview of Scenario 3 (CCGT Power Plant with Post-Combustion Capture)
paragraphs.text: Scenario 3 is a post-combustion chemical absorption arrangement; the chapter covers its process, its interfaces with the CCGT, utilities, layout and full and part load performance. Full performance data are based on 35%wt MEA solvent, which AspenPlus® can model accurately to produce stream data (Appendix D) and equipment sizes. Where relevant, gains possible with proprietary solvents, expected to be widely used by 2020 at the present pace of development, are also noted; these assessments draw on the MHI KM-CDR™ and Siemens PostCap™ systems. Because the vendor data are confidential they are not reproduced, but indicative performance improvements and costs for proprietary systems are given and termed Scenario 3b.

paragraphs.section: 4. Overview of Scenario 3 (CCGT Power Plant with Post-Combustion Capture)
paragraphs.text: Amine scrubbing of flue gas CO2 has so far been used only at small scale compared with what global power sector abatement would need. A recovery plant of roughly 3600 tonnes of CO2 per day requires equipment larger than the scale demonstrated to date (around 500 tonnes of CO2 per day). Parsons Brinckerhoff's view is that every item needed for a large recovery plant has been proven commercially at smaller size or in other services, and that scale-up is a significant but achievable technical challenge.

The post-combustion chemical absorption process has two main parts: absorption, carried out in an absorber column, and desorption, carried out in a stripper (regeneration) column. A simplified block flow diagram is given in Section 4.3 and the full process flow diagram of the capture and compression plant in Appendix A-2. Flue gas fan (4.1.1): a flue-gas fan supplying about 100mbar pressure lift at full load overcomes the capture plant pressure drop and keeps back pressure effects off the GT exhaust; in Scenario 3 it is an axial fan with a 9MW fixed speed (743rpm) drive.

paragraphs.section: 4.1.1 Flue Gas Fan and Direct Contact Cooler
paragraphs.text: Downstream of each fan the flue gas passes through a direct contact cooler (DCC) before absorption. Since absorption is exothermic, the absorber inlet gas should be as cool as possible, so the DCC cools the gas to its water saturation temperature, about 30oC for typical CCGT exhaust. The DCC is a rectangular concrete column in which cooling water is sprayed onto a stainless steel structured packing bed while the gas flows upward; the water is circulated through a heat exchanger that rejects heat to the cooling towers, and condensed water vapour is drawn off at the circulating pump suction.

Cooled gas enters the absorber at the bottom and solvent at the top. Concrete rectangular towers are proposed because, for very large columns (above 18m diameter), they are easier to build on site than cylindrical ones, resemble the rectangular towers of large seawater FGD plants, a commercially proven practice, and the low operating pressure does not demand a cylinder. Good gas and liquid distribution, especially in the corners of a rectangular tower, is the key to achieving the required performance. A counter-flow packed tower is proposed, since structured packing gives low pressure drop, high efficiency, low power use and large contact area compared with spray chambers, venturi scrubbers, ejectors or cross-flow packed scrubbers.

The concrete absorber has a corrosion resistant internal lining and 316L Stainless Steel packing; Scenario 3 assumes Sulzer Mellapak 250Y structured packing at 60% flooding capacity. Sulzer's newer proprietary Mellapak CC packing is noted as reducing pressure drop for a given packing height without losing efficiency. Absorber height is set by the packing height needed for the CO2 separation efficiency, other internals (solvent spray manifolds, water wash, packing supports), free space at the gas inlet for distribution, and the rich solvent sump at the base. Because flue gas CO2 partial pressure is low and 35%wt MEA has lower capacity than proprietary solvents, Scenario 3 needs a column of about 83m. A sterically hindered solvent such as MHI's KS-1 absorbs faster, so less packing is needed for the same CO2, giving a shorter tower and packed section and large CAPEX savings; absorber cross section, however, is governed mainly by limiting gas-side pressure drop and ensuring good gas-solvent contact, so a proprietary solvent changes the footprint less.

Flue gas rises against the descending solvent and about 90% of its CO2 is captured. Solvent that evaporates into the cleaned gas is recovered in a water-wash section at the top of the absorber and returned lower in the column; Siemens' amino acid salt has near-zero vapour pressure, which practically eliminates the need for water wash and saves CAPEX and OPEX. The cleaned gas, mostly nitrogen with excess oxygen and a little CO2, is reheated to 65ºC and released from the top of the absorber. The study proposes using waste heat from stripper reboiler return condensate for this reheat to raise overall efficiency; rotary gas-heaters such as the Ljungström® regenerative type are an alternative but usually leak between clean and dirty gas and add drive power. Reheating ensures adequate plume dispersion, and site-specific air quality modelling will be needed to fix stack location, temperature and height for compliance. CO2-rich solvent exits at the column bottom.

Rich solvent is regenerated in the stripper, where it is heated at low pressure by circulating through a reboiler supplied with LP steam, driving CO2 out. For 35%wt MEA the desorption heat is large because of its high enthalpy of reaction with CO2, a key weakness of MEA; several OEMs offer proprietary solvents that form different reaction products and need roughly 70-80% of MEA's desorption energy. CO2 with traces of solvent leaves the stripper top and the solvent is condensed out. Hot lean solvent from the stripper bottom preheats rich solvent in a lean/rich heat exchanger before returning to the absorber. Structured packing is also proposed for the stripper since in big towers it combines high capacity, a large surface area and little pressure drop, with packing and internals in stainless steel 316 as in the absorber.

A four stage compressor raises CO2 from the stripper to 74bara, with inter-stage coolers and knockout drums collecting condensed water, and a Tri-ethylene Glycol (TEG) dehydrator drying the gas to the Table 4 specification to limit corrosion in transport. Inter-stage cooling uses circulating cooling water from a cooling tower shared by the capture plant. Above the CO2 critical point a final compression stage delivers dense phase CO2 at the assumed pipeline pressure of 110bara.

The main CCGT interfaces in Scenario 3 are LP steam extraction for the capture plant reboilers and diversion of HRSG flue gas to the capture plant. Because the flue-gas fan sits upstream of the direct contact cooler, diverting gas from the HRSG stacks imposes no back pressure on the gas turbine that would reduce its performance. The steam cycle differs from the reference case mainly through the reboiler steam extraction, taken from the MP-LP crossover pipe of the single steam turbine and combined with extra superheated LP steam raised in the HRSG. When the CCS plant is off, surplus steam cannot pass through the ST because of condenser size limits, so the ST cannot be overloaded; the GTs are turned down instead to reduce steam production.

Capture plant condensate typically returns above 120°C and makes up a large share of HRSG feedwater, so the raised low temperature economiser inlet temperature would lift HRSG exit gas temperature by about 15°C versus the reference. The notional design therefore adds a heat exchanger between absorber exit gas (which needs reheating for dispersion) and reboiler condensate, which avoids a leak-prone rotary gas-gas exchanger and substantially lowers the return condensate temperature and hence HRSG exit gas temperature. Main interface items are: diverter/isolation dampers in the HRSG main stacks at the take-off point; exhaust ducting from the HRSG stack to the capture plant; LP steam extraction and supply; electrical supply to the capture plant; and control of both CCGT and capture plant in a common DCS. Shared facility interfaces are raw water treatment and supply to the cooling towers, and fire fighting water.

paragraphs.section: 5. Overview of Scenario 4 (Combined Cycle Plant with Flue Gas Recirculation Post-Combustion Capture)
paragraphs.text: Scenario 4 is a post-combustion scheme with Flue Gas Recirculation (FGR), also called Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR): part of the plant exhaust is returned to the GT compressor inlet and the rest goes to the capture plant. Recycling enriches the CO2 in the gas being treated, which makes capture more efficient and lowers the volume flow to the capture plant, potentially shrinking its size and cost. Apart from this, the capture technology is much the same as Scenario 3, chemical absorption with 35%wt MEA. Leading GT OEMs, notably ALSTOM and General Electric, are actively studying the benefits and effects of FGR for post-combustion capture. The chapter covers process, CCGT interfaces, utilities, layout and full and part load performance.

Section 5.3 gives the simplified block flow diagram and Appendix A-3 the full capture and compression process flow diagram. Fans and coolers (5.1.1): exhaust from each HRSG is split into two streams of equal volume, one returned to that gas turbine's compressor inlet and one sent to capture. Each stream has its own flue gas fan to overcome pressure drop and control flow; flows are to be controlled and balanced by fan inlet-guide vanes, with variable speed drives or extra control dampers possible if finer control is needed. The recycle must not put back pressure on the GT exhaust, which would harm performance, so its control system has to be suitably sophisticated.

paragraphs.section: 5.1.1 Flue Gas Fans and Direct Contact Coolers
paragraphs.text: Each stream passes through a DCC. Recycle gas to the GT air compressor is cooled to 20°C, which improves compression efficiency compared with compressing warm exhaust; the gas leaves the DCC saturated, and a moisture separator removes droplets before it mixes with fresh atmospheric air to form GT combustion air. Gas to the capture plant is cooled to about 30°C as in Scenario 3. Both DCCs are smaller than in Scenario 3 because splitting the flow reduces the volume per column, permitting a cylindrical tower of about 14m diameter, practical to build, and saving about 45% CAPEX per column relative to Scenario 3.

Recirculating flue gas through the gas turbine raises absorber inlet CO2 concentration. Table 18 Comparison of absorber inlet flue gas conditions (Scenario 3 / Scenario 4). Recirculation lifts flue gas CO2 from 4.46%mol (Scenario 3) to 9.03%mol. The richer gas shortens the residence time needed in the absorber, so less packing and a shorter column suffice, and the amine circulation rate can be cut, lowering regeneration heat: Scenario 4's base load stripper reboiler duty is about 248MWth, roughly 92% of Scenario 3's. Smaller gas flow to capture also allows downsizing of the solvent pumps, the lean-rich heat exchangers and the main fans, and capture auxiliary power falls because blower and pump drives are smaller.

GT performance in Scenario 4 is slightly worse than in Scenario 3 because combustion air enters hotter: recycle gas at 20°C mixed with 9°C ambient air gives 14.4°C, 5.4°C above Scenario 3. This costs about 0.6% (point basis) in efficiency, with GT gross LHV efficiencies of 37.98% for Scenario 3 and 37.39% for Scenario 4. Warmer air is less dense, so air mass flow drops and fuel flow is reduced to hold the same air-fuel ratio and flame temperature; running at lower fuel rate behaves like part load, hence the efficiency loss.

Interfaces are largely as in Scenario 3, plus ductwork from the DCC to the GT air intake for recirculation. Recycle gas and fresh air are to be blended in a duct air mixer placed between the GT compressor intake filters and the compressor inlet. The GT combustors may need further modification so that operability, turndown, emissions and combustion efficiency are unchanged compared with fresh-air operation; what such modifications involve is being investigated by the major GT OEMs.

paragraphs.section: 6. Overview of Scenario 5 (Combined Cycle Power Plant with Reforming Plant and Pre-Combustion Capture)
paragraphs.text: Scenario 5 is a pre-combustion scheme: auto-thermal reforming, water gas shift reactions and CO2 removal by physical absorption in Selexol solvent. The chapter explains why the reforming process was chosen, describes the process and the reforming plant/CCGT interfaces, and gives utilities, layout and full and part load performance. No commercial-scale power generation plant yet uses this route, but several studies indicate it is feasible and may beat post-combustion capture, especially by allowing less energy intensive capture methods. It closely resembles proven commercial hydrogen production by natural gas reforming, differing mainly in the added focus on CO2 sequestration and the need to dilute the hydrogen fuel sent to the CCGT. Selexol physical absorption is also used commercially, notably for natural gas sweetening, though at smaller scale. Parsons Brinckerhoff considers all required equipment proven commercially at smaller sizes and in other services, and the scale-up not a huge technical challenge.

Reforming turns the hydrocarbons in natural gas mainly into hydrogen and carbon oxides, usually by catalytic reaction with steam (steam reforming) or with a steam/oxygen mixture (the different adiabatic oxidative reforming routes). Steam reforming (6.1.1): this is the preferred commercial route to hydrogen and proceeds by an endothermic reaction (Equations 6.1 and 6.2).

CxHy + xH_2O(g) ⇌ xCO + (x + y/2)H_2   -ΔH°298 < 0 kJ/mol (6.1) (general steam reforming of a hydrocarbon CxHy to carbon monoxide and hydrogen; the reaction is endothermic). For methane, the main hydrocarbon in natural gas: CH_4 + H_2O ⇌ CO + 3H_2   -ΔH°298 = -206 kJ/mol (6.2) (steam reforming of methane, with the reaction enthalpy term as printed).

Steam reformers scale poorly at large size compared with adiabatic oxidative reformers, and the endothermic reaction needs a large heat input, normally from external combustion. 6.1.2 Adiabatic Oxidative Reforming: here reforming heat comes from burning part of the feed gas internally. Compared with steam reforming this allows much larger single units with better economies of scale and more compact equipment, and higher outlet temperatures give higher conversion. Its main drawback, especially with O2 as oxidant, is the need for an oxygen supply, which usually means large extra investment in air compression, air separation or both.

Given the scale and the importance of overall efficiency, adiabatic oxidative reforming was selected. These processes can be classified by reaction type (homogeneous, e.g. Partial Oxidation or POX; heterogeneous, e.g. Catalytic Partial oxidation or CPO; or both, e.g. Auto-thermal Reforming (ATR) and Secondary reforming), by feed (from a desulphurisation unit or prereformer for POX, CPO and ATR, or partly reformed feed from a fired tubular reformer for secondary reforming) and by oxidant (oxygen, oxygen-enriched air or air). Several commercial-scale ATR plants operate, usually on oxygen, though air-blown units have made synthesis gas for ammonia production.

paragraphs.section: 6.1.2.1 Auto-thermal reforming with air as an oxidant for power production
paragraphs.text: Air as oxidant for power generation syngas avoids the capital and running cost of a large Air Separation Unit (ASU) for oxygen. In addition, the nitrogen in the air passes through the ATR and then dilutes the hydrogen fuel gas, which is needed to limit flame temperature and NOx formation. Air-blown auto-thermal reforming was therefore chosen for this application.

The process was designed to maximise integration between CCGT and reforming plant so the whole plant is as fuel efficient as possible while still reasonably operable. The integrated pre-combustion capture facility comprises a desulphurisation unit, reforming unit, water gas shift reactors and a physical absorption capture unit, supported by efficiency-raising operations such as a furnace pre-heater, absorber solvent chiller and extensive heat recovery exchangers. The flow sheet was developed with Haldor Topsøe, who have previously studied the Integrated Reforming Combined Cycle concept. Section 6.4 gives the simplified block flow diagram and Appendix A-4 the full process flow diagram. Each GT has its own reforming stream to improve overall availability.

Before reforming, the natural gas passes through waste heat recovery exchangers and a pressure reducing station, then through the furnace pre-heater to be heated before desulphurisation. The furnace pre-heater, which raises reforming thermal efficiency, is a five-element fired heater with shared combustion air system and stack; its elements heat separate process streams, including natural gas and reformer process air. It burns process-made hydrogen / nitrogen fuel (around 6t/hr) with some natural gas (around 4t/hr) to limit combustion zone temperature, and has a refractory lining with radiant and convective sections.

Heating the ATR feed with GT exhaust in a dual-purpose HRSG/Waste Heat Recovery Unit was considered but rejected. Combining air/water/steam exchange with air/pressurised flammable gas exchange would change the HRSG's nature, bringing different safety and design codes, much higher cost and fewer willing suppliers. CCGT control and operation would also depart from familiar, well-developed procedures, especially at start-up, leading to more commissioning teething problems, higher risk to CCGT assets and higher insurance premiums, and likely more flaring during start-ups and upsets.

After preheating, desulphurisation is the first process step and a key feedstock purification need, since some syngas preparation catalysts require sulphur at very low levels (ideally single digit ppb) for acceptable life. The usual two-step method hydrogenates organic sulphur compounds and then adsorbs the resulting hydrogen sulphide: feed mixed with a little hydrogen is preheated to about 340°C (via exchangers and the furnace pre-heater), passed through a reactor with hydrogenation catalyst and then a sulphur adsorber, typically zinc oxide. Although the study feed gas (Section 1.7.2) has no sulphur and the step could arguably be left out of the model, the unit is retained because a real plant would not be built without desulphurisation to protect downstream catalysts, and its capital cost share is minimal.

Desulphurised gas is mixed with intermediate pressure process steam at about 46barg, raised in a process steam generator from ATR exit syngas waste heat, then heated to 550°C in the furnace pre-heater (fired on natural gas and hydrogen) ahead of the pre-reformer. Adiabatic pre-reforming is well established and converts the higher hydrocarbons in the feed to carbon oxides and hydrogen, with some unconverted methane and steam remaining, which prevents carbon deposition on catalyst in the main ATR.

Process air for the ATR is bled from the gas turbine air compressor and raised above 43barg by a booster compressor, then preheated to 540°C in the furnace pre-heater; it supplies the oxygen that burns process gas in the ATR combustion zone. Pre-reformer product gas goes straight to the ATR, with a steam to carbon mole ratio of about 1.7. Figure 8 shows the reforming and water gas shift reactions occurring in the downstream thermal and catalytic zone.

CH_4 + 1.5O_2 → CO + 3H_2   -ΔH°298 = 519 kJ/mol (6.3) (the irreversible combustion-zone reaction of methane with oxygen in the ATR, written as printed). Oxygen is the limiting reactant and is entirely consumed in this zone.

Figure 8 caption: Auto-thermal reformer schematic. The syngas outlet pressure was set near the upper end of typical ATR operation, about 40barg, so that the hydrogen fuel gas for the gas turbine needs no recompression and CO2 partial pressure for separation is as high as possible; 40barg was therefore taken as the optimum ATR outlet pressure. At this pressure methane equilibrium conversion falls to about 94% instead of the usual >99%. Efficiency may not suffer, as the methane is still burned in the gas turbine, but CO2 emissions rise because more methane slips into the syngas and is burned there. Reformer syngas holds about 29mol% H2 and about 9mol% CO.

Shift is done in two stages. After a waste heat process steam generator brings the syngas down to about 350°C, it enters the high temperature shift reactor: CO + H_2O ⇌ CO_2 + H_2   -ΔH°298 = 41 kJ/mol (6.4) (water gas shift: carbon monoxide and steam give carbon dioxide and more hydrogen). This yields more hydrogen and lowers CO to about 2.5mol%; after further cooling to about 230°C, the low temperature shift reactor brings CO further down to about 0.5mol%.

paragraphs.section: 6.2.5 Physical absorption of CO2 with Selexol
paragraphs.text: Shifted gas is cooled in a waste heat boiler raising low pressure steam and passes a water knockout drum, leaving at about 16mol% CO2. Joined by gas recycled from the first flash drum, it is fed at about 37barg to the absorber, where it meets chilled lean Selexol at about -10°C; the low temperature keeps solvent circulation low, and structured Mellapak 250Y packing minimises pressure drop. About 93.5% of the feed CO2 is absorbed, giving a fuel gas of about 44%mol nitrogen and 52%mol hydrogen.

paragraphs.section: 6.2.5 Physical absorption of CO2 with Selexol
paragraphs.text: Rich solvent is regenerated and CO2 recovered by flashing at successively lower pressures. A first flash at 8barg and 2°C releases co-absorbed hydrogen and methane, which are compressed and recycled to the absorber. The second flash drum runs at 0.49barg and -4°C, giving vapour of about 96mol% CO2. The solvent then exchanges heat with fully regenerated lean solvent and is warmed with LP steam to about 8.5°C, and this semi-lean solvent is flashed at -0.4barg in the last drum, releasing CO2 of about 99% purity, which is recompressed to 0.49barg and joined with the second-stage vapour. The combined stream (about 97mol% CO2) goes to compression and dehydration, while regenerated solvent is chilled to -10°C in an absorption chiller and returned to the absorber.

A five-stage compressor takes CO2 from the absorption unit to 109barg, with inter-stage cooling and knockout drums removing condensed water; cooling water comes from a cooling tower shared by the capture plant. Before the final compression stage a tri-ethylene glycol (TEG) unit dries the CO2 to below 500ppm water to limit corrosion in the transport system.

Hydrogen fuel gas reaches the gas turbine with an H2:N2 molar ratio of about 55:45, the N2 level being set by adjusting the process air flow to the ATR; nitrogen in the fuel helps restrain NOx formation in the GT. To improve efficiency the fuel is first heated to 78°C with LP steam recovered from syngas cooling before reaching the power block, and then to 230oC with MP economiser water before combustion. In practice the modelled standard GT inlet temperature may have to be de-rated for H2 firing because of higher heat transfer to the blades, slightly lowering overall efficiency, though components developed for high hydrogen combustion may reduce this. The major GT OEMs are working to improve performance on high-hydrogen fuels; GE cites work on combustion, turbine and materials technologies guided by systems analysis of plant-level gains, and reports NOx tests for high hydrogen combustion beyond F-Class conditions.

Burning hydrogen normally requires a larger turbine nozzle area than the reference machine, to pass the higher volumetric fuel flow (hydrogen fuel has lower heat content than natural gas) while keeping design pressure ratios. In Scenario 5, however, the GT compressor is sized to also deliver reforming process air, so the extra fuel volume is balanced by an equal extra air extraction and the overall pressure ratio stays close to the reference without nozzle changes. About 1 tonne/hr of the fuel is blended into the natural gas feed for desulphurisation and about 6 tonne/hr fires the furnace pre-heater; the remainder goes to the gas turbine.

Reforming process air is taken from the GT compressor at about 400°C and used to superheat process steam and the steam exported to the power plant and to raise LP steam for heat exchange. The waste heat IP (intermediate pressure) steam generator is central to reforming heat recovery, producing IP steam at about 49barg from ATR syngas; most serves as ATR process steam, and the surplus is exported to the CCGT for extra power, which makes the STG and condenser larger than otherwise, with some also used for heat exchange within the reformer. Boiler feed water for the heat recovery system comes from the CCGT (with an enlarged feed water system) and cooling water from a shared system. All reasonable efforts were made to use process waste heat to optimise overall net efficiency.

paragraphs.section: 7. Overview of Scenario 6 (Reforming Plant with Pre-Combustion Capture, providing H2/N2 to a Remote Combined Cycle Power Plant & Intermediate Storage)
paragraphs.text: Scenario 6 uses the same pre-combustion route as Scenario 5 (auto-thermal reforming, water gas shift and Selexol physical absorption), but the power plant is remote from the reforming plant and a storage facility is added so H2/N2 fuel can be stored while the power plant is not running, for instance during outages. The chapter gives the reforming selection rationale, process description, interfaces among reforming plant, CCGT and storage site, utilities, layout and full and part load performance. 7.1 Process Description: the reforming plant is assumed 50km from the storage site, which is 5km from the combined cycle plant; H2 / N2 moves by pipeline at around 30 to 40barg, matching reformer operating pressure and GT fuel pressure needs. These distances are arbitrary but considered a reasonable basis. The process largely follows Scenario 5, with differences arising because power plant and reformer cannot be integrated.

As in Scenario 5, feed gas passes through waste heat recovery exchangers and a pressure reducing station, then the furnace pre-heater heats it to 341oC ahead of desulphurisation; inlet conditions to the two-step process and the Hydrogenator and Desulphurisation units are the same as Scenario 5. 7.1.2 Pre-reforming: the treated gas is mixed with process steam at 47barg and 298oC, raised from ATR exit syngas waste heat and then superheated with waste heat from the air compression plant. The mixture is heated to around 550oC in the furnace pre-heater and enters the pre-reformer, which converts higher hydrocarbons to methane, CO, CO2 and hydrogen.

In Scenario 6 a stand-alone air compression plant feeds the ATR, compressing about 343t/hr of ambient air to 46barg (ATR operating pressure). The air leaves at about 347oC and is heated to 540oC in the furnace pre-heater. The five stage air compressor needs 73MW per train in total, a large extra auxiliary load. ATR pressure is as in Scenario 5, with syngas leaving at about 40barg to the process steam generator and shift reactors. 7.1.4 to 7.1.6: the two-stage water gas shift (Section 6.2.4), Selexol physical absorption (Section 6.2.5) and CO2 compression (Section 6.2.6) are identical to the earlier scenario; the compression subsection's text names Scenario 6 as the reference.

As noted in Section 6.3.1, hydrogen firing requires a larger turbine nozzle area to pass the higher fuel volume and hold design pressure ratios. Since Scenario 6 cannot extract GT process air for reforming, the nozzle area is enlarged by 6% relative to the reference to keep design pressure ratios, using GE's standard approach of fitting a Stage 1 nozzle of larger flow area to handle the higher mass flow of syngas operation.

Storage is assumed in a worked-over salt cavern, notionally in the Zechstein salt deposits of NE Netherlands, at 4000ft (1220m) to 6200ft (1890m) depth. Its working capacity is taken as 24bscf (644M Nm^3), about six weeks of base load H2 / N2 output from the reformer, judged sensible to cover a major power plant overhaul; the cavern runs at about 36.1barg with roughly 20bscf (537M Nm^3) of base gas holding pressure. Fuel is compressed to 62barg at the reforming plant and piped to storage (assumed 50km away), with a dedicated 10 MW compressor and a dedicated 36" pipeline per reformer train. Costs covering cavern work-over / leaching, H2/N2 handling plant (compressors plus other top-sides items), storage wells and pipelines are detailed in Section 9.3.5.1.

Waste heat use was again maximised to optimise overall net efficiency. Unlike Scenario 5, surplus ATR steam goes to a stand-alone STG on the reforming site, shared by both trains, instead of boosting the main power plant STG. The Syngas Cooler at the ATR outlet produces IP Steam at 50barg and 265oC at 339.0t/hr; about 40%wt is superheated to 300oC with air compression plant waste heat for process use, and the rest, saturated, drives the stand-alone steam turbine generator, whose 49.8MW gross output offsets part of the process auxiliary load.

With a remote power plant, balance of plant and utility systems that Scenario 5 shares between power and reforming plants must be duplicated. Reforming and power plants each need their own demineralised water treatment, waste water treatment, raw and demineralised water storage, gas reception facilities and buildings, all adding to Scenario 6 CAPEX (see Section 9.3.5).

paragraphs.section: 8.2 Gross Power Output, Net Power Output & Net Efficiency comparison
paragraphs.text: Figure 11 caption: Gross / Net Power Out & Net Efficiency comparison at 100% Load. Table 34 and Figure 11 show net output ranging from 736 to 910 MW. Power block and capture configurations were chosen to give about 800 MW wherever possible, but the auxiliary loads of the various capture technologies differ by up to 190MW, so final outputs vary; power plant auxiliary loads also differ by scenario. Figure 12 caption: Auxiliary Loads comparison at 100% load (power island and carbon capture auxiliary loads).

paragraphs.section: 8.2 Gross Power Output, Net Power Output & Net Efficiency comparison
paragraphs.text: Power plant auxiliary losses are usually around 25MW, covering transformer losses and power for boiler feed pumps, cooling tower pumps, draft fans and the like; for Scenario 6 they also include compressing H2/N2 fuel from storage to the correct GT inlet pressure. Capture and compression loads matter more. In post combustion capture the main electrical loads are the flue-gas fan drives, the CO2 compressor and extra cooling tower pumps and draft fans, and output falls further because LP steam taken from the turbine cross-over for the stripper would otherwise expand through the STG LP section. Relative to the reference plant, output drops by about 121MW for Scenario 3 (35%wt MEA), an efficiency loss of about 8% points; a proprietary solvent system is estimated to lose about 106MW, a 7% point drop. Modelling of Scenario 4 shows a slight efficiency gain over Scenario 3, a 7.5% point drop from the reference (net output reduced by 124.76MW). The results imply the best post-combustion option would pair a proprietary solvent with flue-gas recirculation, though this was not within the study scope.

paragraphs.section: 8.2 Gross Power Output, Net Power Output & Net Efficiency comparison
paragraphs.text: For pre-combustion capture, auxiliary losses include everything in the Reforming Block plus the CO2 Capture and Compression blocks. Scenarios 5 and 6 have far higher losses than the post-combustion cases, mainly because air must be compressed to supply ATR process air. In Scenario 5 this air comes from the GT compressor, sized for both combustion and ATR air, with booster compressor K-002 adding pressure before the ATR. As Scenario 5 is an integrated reforming and power plant, linking the air systems this way saves considerable air compression capital, offset by lower GT efficiency and the operational constraint that the CCGT must start on natural gas before the reformer can start.

paragraphs.section: 8.2 Gross Power Output, Net Power Output & Net Efficiency comparison
paragraphs.text: In Scenario 6 the CCGT is remote, so each stream needs a stand-alone air compressor supplying all process air. The plants can then run independently, but at the price of roughly EUR42M in capital and 145MW of auxiliary load (72.5MW per train). Scenario 6 also needs compression to move H2/N2 from the reformer to storage and on to the CCGT, adding 36.2MW (18.1MW per train), and the stand-alone STG needs its own cooling tower with further auxiliary power. Overall the capture auxiliary load in Scenario 6 is around 165MW above Scenario 5; Table 35 gives an approximate breakdown of the main auxiliary losses for both.
