paragraphs.section: 8.2 Gross Power Output, Net Power Output & Net Efficiency comparison
paragraphs.text: Scenario 6 reaches a net efficiency of 36.8%, 22.0% points below the reference plant and 5.5% points below Scenario 5, so it is not an efficient way to use natural gas for power. Reasons: reforming converts energy at only around 85%, a loss relative to burning gas directly in the CCGT that can be recovered only when the CCGT is co-located with the reformer; the reforming and pre-combustion plant is complex, with many large compressors, pumps and other rotating plant adding auxiliary load; and the storage site serves just one reformer and one CCGT, whereas in practice storage auxiliary loads could be shared among several producers and consumers. Any form of capture, pre or post combustion, adds auxiliary load and lowers efficiency versus the reference; of the options considered Scenario 3b is the most efficient, and flue gas recirculation makes Scenario 4 marginally (0.5% points) more efficient than Scenario 3.

paragraphs.section: 8.3 CO2 Capture Rate & Capture Efficiency comparison
paragraphs.text: Figure 13 caption: CO2 Capture rates and efficiencies comparison at 100% and 40% GT load, for Scenarios 3 to 6. Capture rates are highest in Scenarios 5 and 6 at around 335 t/hr, against 288 t/hr, 289 t/hr and 284 t/hr for Scenarios 3, 3b and 4, but this mainly reflects their greater fuel use (around 2,000 MJ/s LHV versus around 1,500 MJ/s LHV). Capture efficiency is actually higher for post-combustion, around 90% for Scenarios 3 and 4, than for pre-combustion, around 81.5% for Scenarios 5 and 6.

paragraphs.section: 8.3 CO2 Capture Rate & Capture Efficiency comparison
paragraphs.text: Post-combustion chemical absorption removes 90% and pre-combustion Selexol absorption 93.5% of the CO2 entering the absorber. However, pre-combustion plants also fire natural gas and H2 / N2 in the furnace pre-heaters that heat reformer feed gas and process air, and some methane slips through the ATR to the CCGT (GT fuel contains around 1%mol methane, later burned), releasing unabated CO2 and lowering overall capture to 81% for those scenarios. Optimising capture efficiency means balancing plant efficiency, fuel prices, CO2 emission penalties, capital cost, construction and material limits and operating costs. Parsons Brinckerhoff regards the Scenario 5 and 6 capture efficiency as appropriate for this study's scope while noting that more design work could improve it.

Figure 14 caption: Cooling duty comparison at 100% load. Figure 15 caption: Cooling duty comparison at 40% GT load (both split into CCGT and CCP cooling duty). Without capture the base load CCGT cooling duty is 489 MWth, the heat rejected in the condenser by LP turbine exhaust steam and passed to the cooling towers; at 40% load the HRSGs raise less steam and the duty is 318 MWth.

In Scenarios 3 and 4 the total also includes capture and compression cooling. Much of this is heat rejected from condensate returning from the stripper reboiler and flue gas re-heater: effectively, cooling duty moves from the CCGT to the CO2 Capture Block because the reboiler uses LP turbine steam that would otherwise go to the condenser, though at lower enthalpy. Using reboiler condensate waste heat to reheat flue gas before release reduces cooling duty and raises thermal efficiency. The capture and compression block also rejects heat from flue gas cooling in the DCC, surplus heat from lean solvent returning to the absorber (absorption being exothermic) and inter-stage cooling of CO2 compression. In Scenario 5 the CCGT cooling duty is 570.5 MW, about 16% above Scenario 1, because surplus reforming steam exported to the steam turbine increases output and condenser duty; CO2 compression inter-stage cooling adds a further 29 MWth.

Figure 16 caption: Water consumption comparison at 100% load (cooling water, steam cycle make-up and capture plant make-up). Figure 17 caption: Water discharge comparison at 100% load (cooling system blow-down, steam cycle blow-down, DCC, capture unit waste water and demin plant waste water). Most water use in every scenario is cooling tower make-up for the power plant and capture plant, and Scenarios 5 and 6 also use make-up water to raise process steam for reforming. Cooling tower blow-down is a large part of discharge in all cases; post-combustion scenarios also discharge DCC condensate, although for CCGT systems this water should be of fairly high quality and could potentially be recycled elsewhere in the process.

Section 9 gives, for every scenario, an estimate of capital and operating costs that feeds the economic evaluation described in Section 10. Parsons Brinckerhoff produced these estimates on its own, starting from the functional designs set out in the earlier sections and from equipment sizes obtained through performance modelling and discussions with OEM's and other technology suppliers. The capital figures are only estimates, and a competitive tender could deliver lower EPC costs. Sources used for the capital estimates were: recent vendor quotations for the major equipment; out-turn data from reference projects for mature technologies such as thermal and ancillary plant; the PEACE (Plant Engineering and Cost Estimator) module of GT Pro; and Parsons Brinckerhoff's own cost data from many CCS project cost reviews and estimates carried out in 2007-2011 for HM Government (DECC), Australian Federal and State Government and the Global CCS Institute.

Figures are given in current money (2011 costs); reference data from earlier years were escalated at 5% p.a. Everything is expressed in Euros (EUR), and vendor quotes were requested in EUR wherever possible. Assumed exchange rates are 0.75 EUR: 1 USD and 1.14 EUR: 1 GBP, and currency codes follow ISO4217. Total capital cost refers to a turn-key plant on a green-field site supplied under an EPC contract, with an allowance for the EPC contractor's contingency and profit included. Owners costs (for instance in-house feasibility engineering, land purchase, permitting and project finance costs) are shown as a separate item for completeness. The capital cost estimates are considered accurate to within ± 40%.

The costs follow the layout of Table 36, and the terms are explained in the subsections that follow. For every scenario the costs are grouped by broad plant area, such as the Combined Cycle Power Plant, the CO2 Capture Block and the CO2 Compression Block, and a chart of the relative cost of each plant area is also given.

Table 36 Cost Estimate Breakdown (template; columns Area1, Area2, Area3, Area4, Area5 and Total, all in EUR). Row structure: DIRECT MATERIALS = Major Equipment; Piping; Electrical; Control and Instrumentation; Solvents, Catalysts & Other Bulk Chemicals; then SUB-TOTAL DIRECT MATERIALS. MATERIAL / LABOUR CONTRACTS = CIVILS / STEELWORK / BUILDINGS; TANKS AND VESSELS; then SUB-TOTAL MATERIAL & LABOUR CONTRACTS. LABOUR CONTRACTS = MECHANICAL; ELECTRICAL / INSTRUMENTATION; SCAFFOLDING / LAGGING / RIGGING; then SUB-TOTAL LABOUR CONTRACTS. SUB-TOTAL LABOUR & MATERIALS. Other costs = ENGINEERING SERVICES / CONSTRUCTION MANAGEMENT; COMMISSIONING / START-UP; SOFT COSTS CONTRACTOR (Inc Contingency & Profit); SOFT COSTS OWNER; then SUB-TOTAL OTHER COSTS. Final row: TOTAL PROJECT COSTS. The template carries no numerical values.

The 'Direct Materials' item covers all specialised plant equipment delivered to site and equals the total of the major equipment costs for a plant area. For the CCGT power plant it takes in the gas turbines (with combustion systems, starter systems, inlet air filtration and local ancillaries), steam turbines, HRSGs, the condenser and cooling towers, continuous emissions monitoring (CEM), distributed control systems (DCS) and generator- and transmission-voltage equipment. 'Major Equipment' also takes in balance of plant items, for example tanks, pumps, turbine house cranes, the waste water treatment plant and the medium voltage (MV) and low voltage (LV) electrical systems. For a post combustion capture plant, Major Equipment includes the absorbers, strippers, flue gas blowers and every other item that appears in the equipment lists and on the process flow diagram. Within 'Direct Materials', Piping, Control & Instrumentation and the supporting electrical systems are each given their own line. For the Combined Cycle Plant the piping cost comes straight from GT Pro PEACE and covers all pipe-work, while supports and insulation/lagging are counted elsewhere; in the other plant areas these items are taken as a percentage of Major Equipment cost.

The 'Material and Labour Contracts' line groups the remaining major items that are built in place and whose cost mixes materials with labour. A typical example is a civil work package, which bundles materials such as cement, aggregate and reinforcing steel with the labour to build with them. All plant buildings, and steelwork such as racks, supports, access ladders, platforms and walkways for the plant area concerned, are also counted in this line.

The 'Labour Only Contracts' line holds all construction labour for a plant area, divided by trade into 'Mechanical', 'Electrical and Instrumentation' and 'Scaffolding / Insulation / Rigging'. GT Pro PEACE supplies the labour figures for the combined cycle power plant; for every other plant area they are calculated as a percentage of that area's total 'Direct Materials' cost.

'Other Costs' covers engineering and management for EPC delivery, start-up, and the soft costs of both Contractor and Owner. 'Engineering costs' are the Contractor's design work from Feasibility through FEED to detailed construction design, plus EPC project management and site management for the whole project. 'Commissioning / Start-up' covers commissioning labour and management; start-up spares are not in the estimate, and fuel and consumables used in commissioning are handled in the economic model rather than shown here. The 'Contractor's Soft Costs' comprise contingency and profit (applied separately to labour and to equipment), company overheads, bonds and insurances. In this study contingency is taken as 25% on all labour and about 5-10% on Direct Materials, although the perceived risk of price swings in commodities such as steel and copper strongly influences the contingency a contractor would add. Profit is taken as 25% on all labour and about 7% on Direct Materials. These figures depend heavily on location, EPC / OEM market competition and regional labour and material costs, so they should be treated only as estimates that might be bettered. The 'Owner's Soft Costs' comprise owner overheads, project finance costs, insurances, development and legal fees, land purchase or lease, in-house engineering, connection fees and permitting and consenting costs.

paragraphs.section: 9.2.5 Total Plant Costs and Total Capital Requirement Costs
paragraphs.text: Adding up all costs apart from the Owners Soft costs gives the Total Plant Cost (TPC), which can be regarded as the EPC contract price paid by the Owner; a competitively tendered EPC contract could produce a TPC well below the figures in this report. TPC plus the Owners Soft Costs gives the Total Capital Requirement Cost (TCR), which represents the full project cost. The capital costs are overnight costs, so interest during construction (IDC) is excluded here and is instead handled in the economic model (Section 10.3.2).

For the CCGT reference plant (Scenario 1), whose cost summary follows on the next page, the total capital requirement comes to EUR632,125,361, roughly EUR694/kW; excluding the Owners Soft Costs it is about EUR637/kW.

For Scenario 4 the total capital requirement is EUR1,104,241,616, around EUR1,406/kW on a TCR basis and EUR1,285/kW excluding Owners Soft Costs (cost split in Figure 20). Figure 20 CAPEX breakdown for Scenario 4 (segments: Combined Cycle, CO2 Capture Block, CO2 Compression Block). The CO2 Capture Block makes up about 43% of the total capital requirement, against 44% in Scenario 3. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) raises the CO2 concentration of the flue gas, so the 35%wt MEA solvent absorbs CO2 more readily and the absorber columns and their packing can be shorter. Because 50%wt of the flue gas is recirculated, flue gas flowrate and pressure drop also fall, which allows a smaller absorber cross section; together these reduce absorber column CAPEX by an estimated 22% of the corresponding Scenario 3 costs.

These savings are partly offset by the extra flue gas fan, direct contact cooler and ductwork needed to recirculate and condition the flue gas before it returns to the GT compressor, but the study indicates that the savings elsewhere outweigh these added costs. The Scenario 4 estimate does not cover any GT modifications associated with Exhaust Gas Recirculation. Feeding the GT a recirculated stream with lower O2 concentration could harm combustion stability and efficiency, which may call for changes to the machine and/or its combustion systems; OEMs are still carrying out development work to understand the effects of flue gas recirculation.

The H2/N2 storage site was costed as on-shore storage in a salt cavern, notionally in the Zechstein domal salt deposits of NE Netherlands, 4,000 ft to 6,200 ft deep. The cavern is assumed to hold a working capacity of 24bscf (644million Nm^3), about six weeks of reforming plant output, to operate at around 36.1barg, and to keep roughly 20bscf (537million Nm^3) of base gas in place to hold a minimum pressure. The estimate covers work-over / leaching of the cavern, H2/N2 handling (top-sides) equipment, storage wells and pipelines (Table 41). It assumes conversion of domal salt caverns; caverns in bedded salt formations could cost considerably more, and costs also depend on whether suitable formations exist locally. The total capital requirement for the storage site is put at EUR177,225,000. In Scenario 6 the site serves a single reforming plant and a single CCGT, whereas in practice the high cost of gas storage is usually shared across several assets to maximise fleet flexibility and capture electricity and fuel trading opportunities; the scope of the study did not allow these benefits to be explored further.

paragraphs.section: 9.4 Operating cost summary for each scenario
paragraphs.text: Operating costs for each scenario are split into fixed items, such as long term service agreement (LTSA) costs (normally quoted as a fixed cost per fired hour) and routine maintenance, and variable items such as waste disposal and consumables. Assumptions draw on Parsons Brinckerhoff in-house knowledge for established technology like the CCGT plant, and are set as a percentage of TPC where reference projects were not available.

Using Parsons Brinckerhoff data for plants of similar size, Scenario 1 LTSA costs are put at EUR660 per fired hour and CCGT routine maintenance at EUR9.5M per annum. CCGT consumables (boiler feed water treatment and waste water treatment chemicals, lubricants for rotating plant, and raw water consumption & treatment) total an estimated EUR¢2.2/MWh, again based on experience with comparable plant.

Scenario 3 LTSA costs are put at EUR1,132 per fired hour, derived from the scenario's Specific Cost (TPC). Routine maintenance is estimated at EUR16.30M, about EUR10M of which is yearly maintenance of the carbon capture plant according to technology providers. Consumables cover 35%wtMEA solvent make-up, boiler feed water and waste water treatment chemicals, lubricants and raw water consumption & treatment. Solvent make-up is the key item, since MEA degrades and has to be replenished at roughly 1.6kg per tonne of CO2 captured [13]; total consumables are estimated at EUR¢181.53/MWh. Proprietary solvent systems have lower consumable costs than Scenario 3 because the solvent degrades (and is replaced) more slowly, even though proprietary solvents usually cost more than MEA, and slower degradation also cuts waste disposal costs. For Scenario 3b, using averaged supplier data, consumables are estimated at EUR¢136.68/MW/hr, LTSA at EUR959 per fired hour and routine maintenance at EUR13.80M.

Scenario 4 LTSA costs are put at EUR1,034 per fired hour on the basis of its Specific Cost (TPC), and routine maintenance of the whole facility including the CCGT at EUR14.885M. Its consumables (35%wtMEA solvent make-up, boiler feed water and waste water treatment chemicals, lubricants for rotating plant, raw water consumption & treatment) total an estimated EUR¢180.52/MWh.

For Scenario 5, LTSA costs are estimated at EUR1,389 per fired hour from its Specific Cost (TPC). Routine maintenance including the CCGT is estimated at EUR19.99M, which allows for yearly replacement of reforming plant catalysts at roughly 4% of the Reformer block TPC. Consumables comprise Selexol make-up, boiler feed water and waste water treatment chemicals, lubricants and raw water consumption & treatment; boiler feed-water treatment is the major item because the auto-thermal reformer consumes a large amount of process steam. Total consumables are estimated at EUR¢144.73/MWh.

Scenario 6 LTSA costs are put at EUR1,827 per fired hour from its Specific Cost (TPC), and routine maintenance including the CCGT at EUR26.30M, covering yearly replacement of reforming plant catalysts. Consumables are the same categories as Scenario 5 (Selexol make-up, boiler feed water and waste water treatment chemicals, lubricants, raw water consumption & treatment) and total EUR¢219.46/MWh, which reflects the extra rotating plant in this scenario, namely air compressors and the H2/N2 fuel compressors that send fuel to the storage site and the remote CCGT.

Section 10 builds on the baseline technical performance discussed earlier. The technologies compared are: a typical CCGT of 910 MW net output (Scenario 1); a CCGT with Post Combustion Capture, 789 MW net (Scenario 3); a CCGT with Post Combustion Capture using a Proprietary System, 804 MW (Scenario 3b); a CCGT with Post Combustion Capture and Exhaust Gas Re-circulation, 786 MW net (Scenario 4); a CCGT with Natural Gas Reforming and Pre Combustion Capture, 850 MW net (Scenario 5); and Natural Gas Reforming and Pre Combustion Capture with a Remote CCGT, 737 MW net (Scenario 6). The section presents and analyses the lifetime cost of generation of each scenario across a range of plausible values for key drivers such as gas price, carbon price and discount rate, after first describing the calculation method and the base case modelling assumptions.

Parsons Brinckerhoff calculates the lifetime cost of generation with a Discounted Operational Cash Flow (DOCF) model, a common tool for analysing power system costs. The model works out yearly costs for construction and for subsequent operation and maintenance (O&M). Its main cost streams are: capital expenditure (plant EPC, IDC, owners costs, working capital and start up costs); fuel; the cost of CO2 emissions (Carbon Emissions Penalty); CO2 transportation and storage; operating costs (routine maintenance, variable O&M and consumables); and overheads (insurance, salaries, business rates and administrative overheads). Many of these streams depend directly on the plant's expected technical performance, since power output, efficiency, capacity factor and carbon emission or capture rates feed straight into them.

The investments are assumed to be financed 'on the balance sheet' by market participants, which avoids modelling project debt/equity structures. Taxation and capital allowances are ignored, so the results indicate the cost of producing electricity with each technology at the grid connection point. Although the geographic connection point influences the total cost of supplying power to the market, transmission and distribution charges and 'use of system' charges levied by network operators are left out; Parsons Brinckerhoff considers this fair for comparing technologies because such charges vary by country and location. Results are reported per cost component. All future cost streams are treated as evenly spaced and falling at year end, and are discounted with a standard 'year-end' method for consistent comparison. The detailed breakdown shows the make-up of costs in each scenario and the relative contributions between competing technologies, with the typical CCGT plant (Scenario 1) serving as the baseline against which the carbon capture options are compared.

This subsection describes the main base case assumptions used for the lifetime cost of generation; Appendix F summarises them. Data in the DOCF model come from Parsons Brinckerhoff's own information gathered through work in power generation (for developers, financiers or operators), from public documents, or from the IEAGHG report 'Criteria for Technical and Economic Assessment of Plant with Low CO2 Emissions (May 2009)'.

Sections 2 to 7 discuss the technical parameters in detail; Table 42 collects those needed for lifetime cost modelling. Net outputs of the six scenarios lie between 737 MW and about 910 MW. Capacity factor sets the operating hours, and with net output gives annual generation. The typical CCGT (Scenario 1) is assumed to run at 90% in its first year (7884 operating hours) and 93% thereafter (8147 operating hours). The post combustion plants (Scenarios 3, 3b and 4) are assumed at 60% in year one (5238 operating hours) and 90% afterwards, and the pre combustion plants (Scenarios 5 and 6) at 60% in year one and 85% (7446 operating hours) afterwards. These assumptions rest as far as possible on Parsons Brinckerhoff experience with similar plant or on input from technology vendors. Efficiency determines fuel consumption in the DOCF model: the typical CCGT is the most efficient (59% LHV), the post combustion plants follow at around 51 to 52% LHV and the pre combustion plants at around 37 to 42% LHV.

All six scenarios release some CO2 to atmosphere, to differing extents. The reference CCGT (Scenario 1) emits the most, 348 kg of CO2 per MWh. The capture scenarios emit far less: the Post Combustion Capture plants about 40 - 41 kg of CO2 per MWh, roughly a ninth of an unabated CCGT, and the Pre Combustion plants about 89 - 104 kg of CO2 per MWh, around a third or a quarter of a typical CCGT. With no capture equipment, the typical CCGT stores no CO2, whereas the post combustion plants are assumed to store 359 - 365 kg of CO2 per MWh and the pre combustion plants 395 - 454 kg of CO2 per MWh.

Capital expenditure has five parts: the Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) Capital Cost, Interest During Construction (IDC), Owners costs, start up costs and working capital. Table 43 gives the assumptions for each scenario. For lifetime cost modelling the capital costs from Section 9 (cited in the report as 'Section 0') are reduced to two parts: an EPC cost per net kW, and an owners soft cost expressed as a percentage of total EPC cost. The EPC cost in Table 43 is TPC (TCR less Owners Soft costs) divided by net output, and runs from EUR 637 per kW for the typical CCGT to EUR 2421 per kW for the Natural Gas Reforming and Pre-Combustion Capture plant with Remote CCGT. Being overnight costs, these exclude IDC, which the DOCF model computes from the study discount rate (Section 10.3.5) and the disbursement profile. The financial disbursement period means the whole span over which capital is spent, not just physical construction.

The disbursement profile is the same for all scenarios: 15% of capital is spent 4 years before commercial operation, 35% 3 years before, 40% 2 years before and 10% in the final construction year. Owners soft costs are calculated apart from plant expenditure as a share of total EPC cost: 9.0% for the typical CCGT, 9.4% for the post-combustion plants and 10.2% for the pre-combustion plants. The DOCF model books them in the first year of disbursement and they carry no IDC. Every scenario holds enough working capital for 30 days of consumables (boiler feed water treatment and wastewater treatment chemicals, and capture solvents); this is spent in the year before commercial operation and is sized as the theoretical 30-day consumable spend at full load all year.

No working capital is allowed for gas in any option. Scenario 6 (Natural Gas Reforming and Pre Combustion Capture with Remote CCGT) does, however, benefit greatly from storing an intermediate fuel (hydrogen), which adds operational flexibility and opens electricity/fuel trading opportunities (described in Section 7.2.2); the DOCF model does not credit this benefit. Start up expenditure falls in the year before commercial operation and is similar across scenarios: all include one month of maintenance, fuel and consumables start up costs, while labour start up costs equal three months of salaries for Scenarios 1, 3, 3b and 4 and four months for Scenarios 5 and 6, reflecting Parsons Brinckerhoff's estimates of commissioning durations.

O&M costs arise over the whole economic life and consist of variable and fixed routine maintenance plus consumables tied to the energy generated (Table 44). LTSA or Variable O&M (VOM) costs differ widely: the lowest is EUR 660 per fired-hour for the typical CCGT (Scenario 1), while the highest is almost three times as much because of the much greater complexity, the CCGT with Natural Gas Reforming and Pre-Combustion Capture Plant being put at EUR 1827 per fired hour. Routine maintenance shows the same pattern, from EUR 9.5M per annum for the typical CCGT to almost three times that, EUR 26.3M per annum, for the reforming and pre-combustion plant. 'Other Consumables' vary hugely: EUR¢ 2.2 per MWh for the typical CCGT, EUR¢ 137 - EUR¢ 182 per MWh for Scenarios 3, 3B, 4 and 5, and a much higher EUR¢ 219 per MWh for Scenario 6. In the post-combustion plants the solvent dominates, being replaced at around 1.6kg per tonne of CO2 captured; a proprietary solvent may need only about 20% to 30% of the 35%wt MEA replacement rate.

General overheads are taken to include a General Admin Charge, salaries of permanent staff, Business Rates and Insurance. They are incurred every operating year whatever the capacity factor or output, and stay constant in real terms over the economic life. To set them, assumptions were made for the number of permanent staff, their salaries, site rateable values, the national non-domestic multiplier (NNDM), a site-specific general administration charge and a specific insurance cost (Table 45). Staff numbers come from Parsons Brinckerhoff's experience of the technologies, and salaries follow the IEAGHG report 'Criteria for Technical and Economic Assessment of Plant with Low CO2 Emissions (May 2009)'; general administration, business rates and insurance were likewise set from PB's experience.

Business rates equal the assumed rateable value (standing for the open-market annual rent of a non-domestic property) times the national non-domestic multiplier (NNDM, i.e. the pence-in-the-pound rate applied to the rateable value to give the yearly rate bill). The NNDM used is EUR¢ 47.2 per EUR. This parameter is country specific; the model takes the UK 2010/11 figure (GBP pence 41.4 per GBP) and converts it at a EUR to GBP rate of 1.14, since a local value for the study could not be found and it will depend on regional taxation.

All costs are in Euros (EUR and EUR¢) at constant (real) January 2011 prices; inflation is left out on the assumption that it affects every cost equally. Each scenario has a 25 year economic life, as set in the IEAGHG report 'Criteria for Technical and Economic Assessment of Plant with Low CO2 Emissions (May 2009)'. The right discount rate for a project depends on technology maturity, residual project risk and site specific factors; the study baseline is 8%, typical for projects like the reference plant, and higher and lower rates are tested in Section 10.5.4.

Several reputable sources publish international and local gas price forecasts, but gas prices have swung considerably in recent years and past forecasts have often been badly wrong. A varying gas price forecast might be most realistic, yet the future gas price over the study horizon is uncertain. To stay consistent with other IEAGHG studies and let readers compare with earlier work, the base case uses a constant gas price of EUR 6 per GJ (LHV); higher and lower prices are tested in Section 10.5.1.

paragraphs.section: 10.3.7 Carbon Emissions Penalty and the Cost of CO2 Transportation & Storage
paragraphs.text: Every scenario emits some CO2, to differing degrees, and proposed carbon legislation would charge the generator per unit of CO2 emitted. This charge, the 'Carbon Emissions Penalty', is expected to rise in real terms in coming years and will largely be set by policy makers through national and international CO2 reduction targets. For the study the base case penalty is held at EUR 10 per tonne of CO2 emitted, matching EUA (EU allowance) prices at the time. Scenarios 3, 3b, 4, 5 and 6 have capture technology and so emit less CO2 per unit generated than Scenario 1, but incur a variable cost to transport and store the captured CO2, covering the capital and operating costs of the wells and compressors that store it safely. The base case transport and storage cost is a constant EUR 5 per tonne of CO2 stored, agreed with the IEAGHG and in line with 'Criteria for Technical and Economic Assessment of Plant with Low CO2 Emissions (May 2009)'. Sensitivities on the penalty and on transport and storage costs appear in Sections 10.5.2 and 10.5.3.

paragraphs.section: 10.4 Lifetime Cost of Generation - Base Case Results
paragraphs.text: Base case results are given in Tables 46 and 47. The typical CCGT (Scenario 1) has a total lifetime cost of EUR¢ 5.39 per kWh. Fuel dominates at 68% of the total (EUR¢ 3.67 per kWh), followed by capital expenditure at 19.1%; the Carbon Emission Penalty makes up about 6.5%, and O&M plus general overheads the remaining 6.4%. Scenario 3 (CCGT with Post Combustion Capture) comes to EUR¢ 7.66 per kWh, 42% above Scenario 1. Its fuel spend is higher (EUR¢ 4.23 per kWh, mainly because of lower efficiency) and still the main driver, but fuel's share drops to 55.3%. Capital expenditure rises from EUR¢ 1.03 to almost EUR¢ 2.38 per kWh, 31% of the total, reflecting the extra investment in capture and storage facilities. Thanks to capture, the Carbon Emissions Penalty shrinks to only 0.5% of the total, while CO2 transportation and storage adds around 2.4%. O&M and general overheads are much higher than in Scenario 1, at about 10.8% of the total.

paragraphs.section: 10.4 Lifetime Cost of Generation - Base Case Results
paragraphs.text: Scenario 3b (Post Combustion Capture with a Proprietary System) totals EUR¢ 7.07 per kWh: capital expenditure EUR¢ 1.98 per kWh (28%), fuel EUR¢ 4.16 per kWh (58.8%), Carbon Emissions Penalty 0.6%, CO2 transportation and storage 2.5%, and O&M plus general overheads 10.1%. Scenario 4 (Post Combustion Capture with Flue Gas Recirculation) totals EUR¢ 7.41 per kWh, 37% above Scenario 1 but just 3% below Scenario 3, with a cost split close to Scenario 3: fuel 56.8%, capital expenditure 29.5%, CO2 emissions 0.5%, CO2 transportation and storage 2.4%, and O&M plus general overheads about 10.7%.

paragraphs.section: 10.4 Lifetime Cost of Generation - Base Case Results
paragraphs.text: Scenario 5 (CCGT with Natural Gas Reforming and Pre Combustion Capture) totals EUR¢ 9.17 per kWh, about 70% above Scenario 1 and roughly 20%, 30% and 24% above Scenarios 3, 3b and 4 respectively. Fuel spend exceeds that of Scenarios 3, 3b and 4 (EUR¢ 5.11 per kWh, mainly owing to lower efficiency) and still drives the total, though its share is a smaller 55.7% than in Scenario 1. Capital expenditure rises above Scenarios 1, 3, 3b and 4 to EUR 2.88 per kWh (as printed), although at about 31.4% its share is similar to Scenario 3; this reflects the greater investment for pre-combustion compared with post-combustion technology. With capture fitted, the Carbon Emissions Penalty is far below a typical CCGT but not as low as in Scenarios 3, 3b and 4, at 1% of the total or EUR¢ 0.09 per kWh. CO2 transportation and storage adds about 2.2% and O&M plus general overheads 9.8%.

paragraphs.section: 10.4 Lifetime Cost of Generation - Base Case Results
paragraphs.text: Scenario 6 (Natural Gas Reforming and Pre Combustion Capture with remote CCGT) has a lifetime cost of EUR¢ 11.80 per kWh, about 119% above Scenario 1, about 54% above Scenario 3, about 67% above Scenario 3b, 59% above Scenario 4 and 29% above Option 5. Fuel's share is the lowest of the six at only 49.8%, yet the actual fuel spend is the highest at EUR¢ 5.88 per kWh, more than the whole lifetime cost of a typical CCGT. The additional facilities push the capital expenditure contribution to around EUR¢ 4.35 per kWh (36.8%). CO2 emission costs are similar to Scenario 5 at around 0.9%, and CO2 transportation and storage, at about EUR¢ 0.23 per kWh, is similar to Scenarios 3 to 5 but only 1.9% of the total. O&M and general overheads make up 10.5%.

paragraphs.section: 10.4 Lifetime Cost of Generation - Base Case Results
paragraphs.text: From the base case charts, the scenarios rank from lowest to highest total lifetime cost of generation as: 1. Scenario 1 - Reference CCGT Plant; 2. Scenario 3b - CCGT with Post Combustion Capture using a typical Propriety System; 3. Scenario 4 - CCGT with Post Combustion Capture (35%wt MEA) and FGR; 4. Scenario 3 - CCGT with Post Combustion Capture (35%wt MEA); 5. Scenario 5 - CCGT with Natural Gas Reforming and Pre Combustion Capture; 6. Scenario 6 - Natural Gas Reforming and Pre Combustion Capture with Remote CCGT.

Sensitivity runs examine how far shifts in key inputs move each scenario's total lifetime generation cost and its competitiveness against the others: changes in gas price, in the Carbon Emissions Penalty, in CO2 transportation and storage cost, in discount rate, and in plant capacity factor. The subsections below give the results, and Appendix G has summary graphs of all sensitivities for each scenario.

Gas price sensitivity uses a low price of EUR 3 per GJ LHV and a high price of EUR 12 per GJ LHV (Tables 48 and 49). Halving the gas price lowers every lifetime cost: Scenario 1 becomes EUR¢ 3.54 per kWh, the post combustion options (Scenarios 3, 3b and 4) about EUR¢ 4.97 – 5.52 per kWh, and Scenarios 5 and 6 EUR¢ 6.59 and EUR¢ 8.83 per kWh. Doubling it raises every cost: Scenario 1 reaches EUR¢ 9.09 per kWh, Scenarios 3, 3b and 4 EUR¢ 11.93, EUR¢ 11.26 and EUR¢ 11.65 per kWh, and Scenarios 5 and 6 EUR¢ 14.32 and EUR¢ 17.73 per kWh. All scenarios are therefore very sensitive to gas price, but the ranking stays as in the base case because of the plant efficiencies and fuel consumption characteristics. Gas price mainly moves the fuel component but also slightly changes capital expenditure, since the capital figure includes a fuel start-up cost whose size follows the fuel price. paragraphs.section: 10.5.2 Changes to the Carbon Emissions Penalty
paragraphs.text: The Carbon Emissions Penalty was tested at EUR 0, EUR 50 and EUR 100 per tonne of CO2 emitted (Tables 50 to 52). Having the highest CO2 emissions per kWh, Scenario 1 gains most when the penalty is removed, its total falling by EUR¢ 0.34 to EUR¢ 5.05 per KWh, while the capture options, emitting less, see smaller reductions; Scenario 1 thus becomes relatively more attractive than in the base case. The effect reverses at EUR 50 per tonne, where Scenario 1's lifetime cost rises more than those of the capture scenarios, and at EUR 100 per tonne Scenario 1 is no longer cheapest, with Scenarios 3, 3b and 4 all below it. A breakeven analysis found the penalty at which Scenarios 3, 3b, 4, 5 and 6 reach a lifetime cost equal to or below Scenario 1 (Table 53). Scenario 1's lifetime cost is clearly more sensitive to the carbon emissions penalty than those of the capture-equipped scenarios. Figures 27, 28 and 29 chart these sensitivities.

paragraphs.section: 10.5.3 Changes to the Cost of CO2 Transportation and Storage
paragraphs.text: This sensitivity looks at two cases: no charge at all for CO2 transportation and storage (for instance where the captured CO2 can be sold for reuse), and a high charge of EUR 10 per tonne of CO2 stored (Tables 54 and 55). Scenario 1 is unaffected since it stores no carbon, but the relative competitiveness of the capture scenarios against Scenario 1 shifts. With zero cost, every capture option gains on Scenario 1, and Scenario 6 benefits most, narrowing the gap to the other capture technologies though it remains by far the most expensive. With the higher cost the reverse happens: Scenario 6, capturing the most CO2, sees the largest increase and loses ground to the other capture options, while all capture options lose ground to Scenario 1. In this study these changes are small compared with the total lifetime costs. Figure 30 Lifetime Cost of Electricity (EUR¢ per kWh) - Zero CO2 Transportation and Storage Cost. Discount rate was tested at a low 5% and a high 10% (Tables 56 and 57). It affects only the capital expenditure component. A lower rate reduces the capital component for every scenario, and because all scenarios share the same disbursement schedule, the reduction is larger for plants with higher capital cost, so high-capital scenarios become more competitive against low-capital ones. A higher rate does the opposite, raising the capital component faster for high-capital plants and favouring the lower capital cost scenarios. Within the range examined, the discount rate does not materially alter the base case conclusions and the ranking by total lifetime cost is unchanged. Because flexible operation is a major advantage of gas-fired plant, the lifetime cost was also evaluated at capacity factors of 50% and 25% (Tables 58 and 59). The capacity factor changes annual operating hours; this alters O&M and general overhead spending, which usually scale with fired hours, but the effect of these streams on lifetime cost is minor. The large effect is on the capital component and the total: lifetime cost per kWh is all costs divided by lifetime generation, so the more a plant runs, the more hours there are to recover its capital. Lower capacity factors keep capital spending fixed while cutting generation, raising the capital share, and more so for high-capital plants, so these become less competitive than low-capital plants as capacity factor drops. The totals change considerably, but the ranking is the same. Figure 34 Lifetime Cost of Electricity (EUR¢ per kWh) - 50% Capacity Factor. Figure 35 Lifetime Cost of Electricity (EUR¢ per kWh) – 25% Capacity Factor.

Scenario 6 deserves particular comment here: the results show that the CAPEX of the reformer plant and storage site makes it uncompetitive in a 1:1 configuration, especially at low capacity factors. The authors suggest the advantages of natural gas reforming and hydrogen storage would be better exploited if one reforming plant and its storage served several CCGTs. The reforming plant would then run at base-load for best efficiency while the CCGTs operate flexibly, and reforming and storage CAPEX would be spread over several CCGT's, lowering its share of the levelised cost of generation below the values shown and potentially cutting specific costs (EUR/kW) for low load plants. This lies outside the study scope, but further analysis is judged worthwhile.

With base case assumptions, the lifetime cost modelling shows Scenario 1 as the preferred option on lowest total lifetime cost, although this headline hides several other relevant findings from the analysis.

Main base case conclusions: ranked by lowest total lifetime cost of generation, the order is 1. Scenario 1 (EUR 5.39 per kWh); 2. Scenario 3b (EUR 7.07 per kWh, 31% above Scenario 1); 3. Scenario 4 (EUR 7.41 per kWh, 37% above); 4. Scenario 3 (EUR 7.66 per kWh, 42% above); 5. Scenario 5 (EUR 9.17 per kWh, 70% above); 6. Scenario 6 (EUR 11.80 per kWh, 119% above) (units printed as EUR per kWh). Fuel is the biggest contributor in every scenario, about 50 - 68% of the total. Fuel cost per kWh is higher with capture because the lower efficiency means burning more fuel for the same output, yet fuel's percentage share is smaller in the less efficient scenarios, mostly because of the added capital cost of capture. Capital expenditure is the second biggest contributor, about 19 - 37%; its cost per kWh is naturally higher with capture since capture adds capital cost at similar net output, and its share is larger for Pre Combustion Capture plant (around 31 – 37%) than for Post Combustion Plant (28 – 31%), compared with 19% for a typical CCGT. O&M and general overheads take around 9.8 – 10.7% of the total in capture scenarios against 6.4% for the typical CCGT.

Lacking capture, the typical CCGT (Scenario 1) emits more CO2 per kWh, so the Carbon Emissions Penalty affects its lifetime cost more than it affects the capture plants; those plants, however, pay for safe and secure transportation and storage of the captured CO2, which partly cancels their penalty savings. The cost of carbon (emissions penalty plus transport and storage) is analysed in Table 60. At the base case prices (EUR 10 per tonne of CO2 emitted and EUR 5 per tonne of CO2 stored), Pre Combustion Capture plant (Scenarios 5 and 6) cannot compete with typical CCGT or even Post Combustion Capture plant. Scenario 1 pays only EUR 0.35 per kWh of penalty and nothing for storage, while Scenarios 5 and 6 pay about EUR 0.09 - 0.10 per kWh of penalty and EUR 0.20 - 0.23 per kWh for transport and storage, so their total carbon cost (EUR 0.29 – 0.33) is only slightly below the typical CCGT (EUR 0.35 per kWh). Even the post combustion options carry EUR 0.22 per kWh. Given the much larger fuel and capital spend of capture plant, there is little room at base case penalty and storage prices for capture technologies to compete with a typical CCGT (units printed as EUR per kWh).

Sensitivities were run on gas price, Carbon Emissions Penalty, CO2 transportation and storage cost, discount rate and power plant capacity factor; the main conclusions are listed in the following subsections.

Since fuel is the largest lifetime cost component in every base case scenario, gas price changes strongly affect the results. At EUR 3 per GJ LHV the ranking stays the same, but cheaper fuel lessens the penalty of lower efficiency on fuel spending, making the capture scenarios relatively more attractive against Scenario 1. At EUR 12 per GJ LHV the ranking again stays the same, but dearer fuel magnifies the effect of lower efficiency, so Scenario 1 becomes relatively more attractive than the capture scenarios.

A lower Carbon Emissions Penalty widens the lifetime cost gap between Scenario1 and the scenarios with capture and storage, and a higher penalty narrows it. The ranking is unchanged at EUR 50 per tonne of CO2 emitted, but at EUR 100 per tonne it changes, with Scenarios 3, 3b and 4 all cheaper than Scenario 1. Breakeven analysis shows the penalty would need to reach EUR 80 - 90 per tonne for Scenario 3, EUR 60 - 70 per tonne for Scenario 3b, EUR 70 - 80 per tonne for Scenario 4, EUR 150 - 160 per tonne for Scenario 5 and EUR 270 - 280 per tonne of CO2 emitted for Scenario 6 to become more attractive than Scenario 1.

The cost of CO2 transportation and storage does not affect Scenario 1's total lifetime cost, but it does change how competitive the capture scenarios are against Scenario 1: cheaper transport and storage makes all capture options more competitive with Scenario 1, and dearer transport and storage makes them less so.

With a lower discount rate the capital cost per kWh falls faster for high-capital plants, improving the competitiveness of high capital cost scenarios against cheaper ones; with a higher discount rate it rises faster for high-capital plants, so lower capital cost scenarios gain against the higher capital cost ones.

Reducing the capacity factor raises the capital cost per kWh, because capital spending is fixed while total generation falls. The effect is stronger for plants with higher capital costs, so as capacity factor drops these scenarios lose competitiveness against plants with lower capacity factors (wording as printed in the report). The capacity factors examined change the total lifetime costs considerably, but the ranking of alternatives stays the same.

paragraphs.text: SPECCA = (HR - HR_ref) / (E_ref - E) (extra heat rate needed per unit of CO2 emission avoided, relative to the same plant without CCS), where HR is the plant heat rate in kJ_LHV/kWh, E is the CO2 emission rate in kgCO2/kWh, and the subscript ref denotes the value for the same plant without CCS.

paragraphs.section: 11.1.1 Impacts of CCS technology on the net efficiency of gas-fired power plant
paragraphs.text: The results show that CO2 capture on gas fired plants of any type costs between 7% points and 22% points of overall efficiency, and that of the two main capture routes, post-combustion technology is markedly more efficient. Because combined cycle gas-fired CCGT plants are among the most efficient ways of generating power, with typical net efficiencies of 50-60%, the authors judge gas plant a sensible choice for near-term demonstration of post-combustion CCS technology.

paragraphs.section: 11.1.2 Impacts of CCS technology on the capital cost of gas-fired power plant
paragraphs.text: Figure 37 Comparison of capital cost breakdown for each scenario (Cost in EUR million for Scenarios 1, 3, 3b, 4, 5 and 6, split into Combined Cycle, CO2 Capture, Reforming, CO2 Compression, Common Facilities, and Storage Reservoir and topsides). New gas plants fitted with CO2 capture need substantial capital compared with unabated plant. Among the capture scenarios, post-combustion capture with a typical proprietary solvent system (Scenario 3b) needs the least total plant capital. Between the two 35%wt MEA cases, the layout with flue-gas recirculation (Scenario 4) costs less, a marginal gain over capture without FGR (Scenario 3). Parsons Brinckerhoff considers that GT OEM's should develop and demonstrate this technology further to understand fully how FGR affects combustion efficiency and GT performance. In principle the results point to an optimal post-combustion solution combining a proprietary solvent with flue-gas recirculation.

paragraphs.section: 11.1.2 Impacts of CCS technology on the capital cost of gas-fired power plant
paragraphs.text: Scenario 6 (natural gas reforming with a remote CCGT and intermediate fuel storage) is judged not to be a realistic near-term option for base-load gas-fired generation. One reason is its configuration: the storage site, which adds some EUR180million of capital, serves only one reforming plant and one CCGT, whereas in practice such storage costs are usually shared among several assets. In addition, the economic modelling ignores extra revenue from electricity / fuel trading, which might improve the economics of this scenario.

paragraphs.section: 11.1.3 Impacts of CCS technology on the lifetime electricity cost for gas-fired power plant
paragraphs.text: The conclusion drawn is that the Carbon Emissions Penalty would have to rise to EUR 60 - 80 per tonne of CO2 emitted for post-combustion capture to become commercially viable, and to EUR 150 - 270 per tonne of CO2 emitted for natural gas reforming with pre-combustion capture to do so.

Gas fired generation will be vital in the future energy mix because natural gas is plentiful and emits relatively little compared with fuels such as coal. Large near-term investment in new gas capacity is expected to replace ageing plant forced to retire by environmental legislation such as LCPD and IED and by new emissions performance standards. In the long term gas plant is expected to provide the generation flexibility that could otherwise be limited by the variability of the high levels of renewables needed to meet global emissions targets. Demonstrating CO2 capture on gas-fired plant in the near term is therefore important so that it can be rolled out globally between 2020 and 2050. The report finds that Gas + CCS lowers overall plant efficiency considerably, typically by about 7% points for post-combustion capture, and that the lifetime cost of electricity with post-combustion capture is around EUR¢ 7/kWh – EUR¢ 8/kWh, against around EUR¢ 5/kWh for conventional, unabated CCGT.

Natural gas reforming to make hydrogen with pre-combustion CO2 capture is judged not viable for power generation in the near term, and post-combustion capture is seen as the most realistic route to abating CO2 from power plants. Costs of Gas + CCS are expected to fall as the technology is deployed; since fuel dominates the lifetime cost in these scenarios, the authors see optimisation and improvement of net efficiency as the fastest path to cost reduction. Even allowing for future cost reductions, widespread deployment of Gas + CCS at the scale needed to cut power sector CO2 emissions would require a strong carbon emissions penalty of at least EUR 60 / tCO2.

paragraphs.section: Appendix H: Siemens Post-Combustion Capture Process
paragraphs.text: Appendix H describes the Siemens PostCap process, a second generation post-combustion CO2 capture technology that Siemens tailored for integration into both combined cycle plants and conventional coal-fired units. Development began about five years before the report and is based on amino acid salt solvent formulations. In choosing the solvent, Siemens set as leading criteria that solvent and process be simple to handle, add no new emissions and stay within existing power plant safety standards, while capture efficiency, energy demand and solvent make-up needs were expected to clearly beat current standards. Because amino acid salt solutions are ionic, the solvent resists oxygen degradation very well, which matters because NG-CCPP flue gas carries more oxygen than coal plant flue gas; thousands of hours of laboratory and pilot plant testing are cited as confirming these properties.

paragraphs.section: Appendix H: Siemens Post-Combustion Capture Process
paragraphs.text: Emission tests at the pilot unit at the Staudinger coal-fired power station found no detectable solvent or nitrosamine salt emissions at the absorber top, so no extra wash stages are needed for the absorber off-gas. Degradation products formed by side reactions with flue gas trace components stay in the liquid and can be collected and removed in the re-claimer; the two step reclaiming is said to be far more selective than the re-boiling systems of amine based processes, and sulphur components are separated and converted into an industrial product. The solvent's handling, transport and storage needs follow from its properties: it is not flammable ('neither inflammable, nor explosive'), has no odour and poses no inhalation risk, and since its components occur naturally the risk to people, fauna and flora is very low. Siemens considers PostCap ready for large-scale units and points to its in-house chemical process engineering and other power station disciplines for implementation.

부록 B-2 Scenario 3 CO2 Compression 장비목록(PDF p.199)의 CO2 Compressor Package 'T Mech Des' 칸은 'Stage 1: 150/-10 Stage 2:'로 인쇄가 잘려 있어 그대로 기재; 일부 Flowrate 칸('H: C: 2294 t/h' 등)도 인쇄된 칸 구성 그대로

부록 B 장비목록 Comments 칸의 긴 비고 일부는 paraphrase로 줄여 씀(수치·기호 유지); 원문 오탈자 'lenghth', 'Estmated', 'pakage', 'recirculaton'은 교정, 'Control and Instrumentiaton'(비용표), 'REFERANCE'(C-1 도면명), 'SENSITIVITIY'(부록 G 제목)는 인쇄 철자 그대로
부록 B/D 표는 pdfplumber 표 추출 결과를 사용했고 CO2/H2O 등 아래첨자가 'CO 2'로 분리된 것을 복원함; 수치는 pdftotext 원문과 자동 대조(모든 수치 일치)
부록 D-1 Scenario 3 Stream 1 Flue Gas to DCC 온도 '97.05*'의 별표에 대응하는 각주는 페이지에 없음 → 별표 포함 그대로 기재
부록 E-1: Scenario 3/3b 시트는 요약 박스에 Net electric efficiency(HHV)·Plant auxiliary 줄이 없고, Scenario 5/6 시트는 HHV·용수 줄이 없음(인쇄 그대로). 시나리오와 부하는 각 시트의 모델 파일명으로 판별
부록 F의 'Capital Disbursements (% of total)' 행 값은 모든 열이 'ok'로 인쇄됨(점검 표시로 보임); 'Owners, Working and Start Up Costs' 머리행 값은 0으로 인쇄됨
부록 A-3/A-4/A-5의 CO2 Compression PFD는 Scenario 3과 같은 도면번호 64225A-DSC-00003(Rev 1)이 재사용됨(인쇄 그대로)
